topics.title: Software Process Models
topics.summary: The generic process framework, umbrella activities, process patterns, and every prescriptive model from waterfall to the Unified Process with the situation each one fits.

blocks.text:
## Why a process at all

Software is not manufactured; it is *engineered*, and it does not wear out — it deteriorates because of repeated change. Those two facts mean that the risk in a software project is almost never the typing. It is agreeing what to build, keeping the design coherent while requirements move, and knowing when the thing is good enough to ship. A **software process** is the framework of activities, actions and tasks that a team follows to get from an idea to a deployed, maintained product. A **process model** is a named, prescriptive arrangement of that framework: which activities happen, in what order, how often, and what comes out of each.

The vocabulary is layered and the exam tests the layering directly:

- A **process framework** contains a small number of **framework activities** that apply to every project, large or small.
- Each framework activity contains **software engineering actions** (for example, *architectural design* is an action inside modelling).
- Each action is a set of **work tasks**, each producing **work products**, with **quality assurance points** and **project milestones**.
- Running alongside all of it are the **umbrella activities**, which are not tied to any one phase.

blocks.title: The five generic framework activities
blocks.text:
**Communication → Planning → Modeling → Construction → Deployment.**

Remember **C-P-M-C-D**. Communication is requirements gathering and customer collaboration; Planning produces the software project plan (tasks, risks, resources, schedule); Modeling covers analysis and design; Construction is code generation *and* testing together; Deployment is delivery, support and feedback.

A common exam distractor puts *testing* as a sixth framework activity. It is not — testing lives inside **Construction**.

## Umbrella activities

Umbrella activities run across the whole life cycle rather than at one point in it. Pressman's list has eight:

1. Software project tracking and control
2. Risk management
3. Software quality assurance
4. Technical reviews
5. Measurement
6. Software configuration management
7. Reusability management
8. Work product preparation and production

If a question asks whether *risk management*, *SQA*, *measurement* or *SCM* is a framework activity or an umbrella activity, the answer is always umbrella. The framework list has exactly five entries and none of them is a management or assurance function.

## Process patterns

A **process pattern** describes a recurring process problem, the context it occurs in, and a proven way of addressing it — the same idea as a design pattern, applied one level up. Ambler's template names the pattern, its **forces**, its **type**, the **initial context**, the **problem**, the **solution**, the **resulting context**, **related patterns** and **known uses**.

Three pattern types, in order of increasing scope:

| Type | Scope | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Task pattern** | one action or work task | *TechnicalReview*, *RequirementsGathering* |
| **Stage pattern** | one framework activity, may contain task patterns | *Communication*, *DesignTheSolution* |
| **Phase pattern** | the sequence of activities for the whole project | *SpiralModel*, *Prototyping* |

## Process assessment and maturity

A process that is never measured cannot be improved. **CMMI** (Capability Maturity Model Integration) grades organisational process maturity in five staged levels:

| Level | Name | Characteristic |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Initial | ad hoc, heroic, unrepeatable |
| 2 | Managed | project-level discipline; requirements management, planning, tracking, SCM, QA |
| 3 | Defined | one tailored organisation-wide standard process |
| 4 | Quantitatively Managed | process and quality controlled statistically |
| 5 | Optimizing | continuous, measured improvement and defect prevention |

The continuous representation instead rates each process area on capability levels 0–5 (Incomplete, Performed, Managed, Defined, Quantitatively Managed, Optimizing). Other assessment vehicles are **SCAMPI**, **CBA IPI**, **SPICE (ISO/IEC 15504)** and **ISO 9001:2000**. Individual and team variants are the **Personal Software Process (PSP)** and **Team Software Process (TSP)**.

## The prescriptive models

A **prescriptive** model prescribes the order and the deliverables in advance. They differ almost entirely in *when requirements are allowed to change* and *how early the customer sees running code*.

### Waterfall (classic life cycle, Royce 1970)

Communication → Planning → Modeling → Construction → Deployment, each completed and signed off before the next begins. Documents are the hand-off between phases. It works only when requirements are fixed, well understood and stable, the technology is familiar, and the work is essentially a well-defined adaptation of an existing system.

Its three classic weaknesses: real projects rarely follow a strict sequence; the customer must state every requirement up front and then wait; and no working version exists until very late, so a large blunder is discovered at the worst possible moment. Blocking states — where members wait on each other's documents — are common.

### V-model

The waterfall bent into a V. The descending left arm is specification and decomposition; the ascending right arm is integration and testing; coding sits at the vertex. Each level of specification is paired with the test level that validates it:

| Left arm (verification) | Right arm (validation) |
|---|---|
| Requirements analysis | Acceptance testing |
| System / architectural design | System testing |
| Component / high-level design | Integration testing |
| Module / detailed design | Unit testing |

The V-model contributes nothing new about sequencing — it is still a waterfall — but it makes the point that **test plans are written when the corresponding specification is written**, not at the end.

### Incremental model

Apply linear sequences in a staggered fashion, each producing a deliverable **increment**. The **first increment is the core product**: the essential functionality, with the extras left out. Customer feedback on increment $n$ shapes increment $n+1$. Useful when staffing is unavailable for a full release, or when the customer must have *something* operational by a fixed date. Distinguish it from *iterative*: incremental adds function; iterative refines the same function.

### RAD (Rapid Application Development)

An incremental model with an extremely short cycle — a **60 to 90 day** delivery window — achieved by component reuse and code generation. Its phases are **business modelling, data modelling, process modelling, application generation, testing and turnover**. Multiple teams work on separate functional scopes in parallel.

RAD fails when: the system cannot be properly modularised; the application demands high performance tuned at interfaces; the technical risk is high; or the customer and developers cannot commit to the rapid-fire activity the timebox requires.

### Prototyping

Build a quick mock-up — often only screens and navigation — to pin down requirements the customer cannot articulate or an algorithm whose efficiency is uncertain. It is not a stand-alone life cycle so much as a technique that can be dropped into any other model. Cycle: communication → quick plan → quick design modelling → construct prototype → deployment, delivery and feedback, repeat.

The danger is political: the customer sees something that works and asks to ship it, and the developer, having used the first language that came to hand and ignored quality, agrees. A **throwaway** prototype must actually be thrown away; an **evolutionary** prototype must be built to production standards from the start.

### Spiral model (Boehm, 1988)

Couples the iterative nature of prototyping with the control of the waterfall, and makes **risk the driver**. The project spirals outward through the same set of task regions, each circuit producing a more complete version — a paper model first, then a prototype, then successively more complete engineered systems. Boehm's original four quadrants are:

1. Determine objectives, alternatives and constraints
2. Evaluate alternatives; identify and resolve risks
3. Develop and verify the next-level product
4. Plan the next phase

Key properties: it is the **only classical model with explicit risk analysis in every cycle**; it does not end at delivery — the spiral continues through maintenance; and the radius of the spiral represents cumulative cost while the angular dimension represents progress through one circuit. It needs genuine risk-assessment expertise, and it suits large, expensive, high-risk systems. The **WINWIN spiral** adds an explicit customer–developer negotiation region.

### Concurrent development model (concurrent engineering)

Recognises that in a real project the framework activities do not queue; they all exist simultaneously, each in a different **state**. Modelling might be *under development* while a piece of it is *awaiting changes* and another is *under review*. Typical states of an activity are: none, under development, awaiting changes, under review, under revision, baselined, done. Transitions are triggered by events elsewhere in the project. It is applicable to all software development and is especially natural for client/server work.

### Component-based development

Treats commercial off-the-shelf and in-house components as the unit of construction. The steps are: research and evaluate candidate components; consider integration issues; design an architecture to accommodate them; integrate components into the architecture; test thoroughly. It has the evolutionary, iterative character of the spiral, and its pay-off is measured in reuse: reported figures of the order of 70% reduction in development cycle time and 84% of project cost.

### Formal methods model

Specify the system in a mathematical notation (**Z**, **VDM**, **B**) and refine the specification into code by correctness-preserving transformations, so that ambiguity, incompleteness and inconsistency are discovered by analysis rather than by testing. **Cleanroom software engineering** is the best-known instance. It is extremely time-consuming and expensive, demands training few developers have, and is hard to use as a customer communication tool — so it is reserved for safety-critical and security-critical systems.

### Aspect-oriented software development (AOSD)

Some concerns — security, logging, persistence, fault tolerance — cut across many components and cannot be localised in any one module. AOSD names these **crosscutting concerns**, represents each as an **aspect**, and *weaves* aspects into the system at defined join points. AOSD is a distinct process *and* a design/programming discipline; it is still maturing and is usually layered onto an evolutionary process.

### The Unified Process (UP / RUP)

Use-case driven, architecture-centric, iterative and incremental; developed alongside UML by Jacobson, Booch and Rumbaugh. Its phases are:

| Phase | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Inception** | business case, scope, rough architecture, key use cases |
| **Elaboration** | refine use cases, produce an executable architectural baseline |
| **Construction** | build the remaining components; the bulk of coding and testing |
| **Transition** | beta release, user feedback, training, deployment |
| **Production** | ongoing monitoring and support (Pressman's generic UP adds this) |

Remember the order **I-E-C-T**. A frequent question asks in which phase the architecture is baselined: **Elaboration**, not Construction.

blocks.title: Worked example — choosing a model from the symptoms
blocks.text:
Read each situation and name the single best-fitting prescriptive model. The exam asks exactly this, usually as a match-the-list.

**(a)** A bank must replace a 20-year-old fixed-deposit interest calculator. The rules are published by the regulator, will not change during the project, and the team has built three similar systems.
→ **Waterfall.** Stable, fully understood requirements plus familiar technology is the *only* situation waterfall genuinely fits.

**(b)** A defence contractor is building flight-control software where a residual fault could kill. Budget and schedule are generous.
→ **Formal methods model** (Cleanroom). Correctness must be demonstrated, not sampled.

**(c)** A start-up's founder can describe the feel of the product but cannot say what the reports should contain until she sees some.
→ **Prototyping.** Requirements are fuzzy on the customer side, not the technical side.

**(d)** A 200 person-month project with a new database technology nobody in the firm has used, an uncertain integration with a partner's API, and a board that wants the risk reviewed at each funding gate.
→ **Spiral.** Large, expensive, high technical risk, repeated go/no-go decisions.

**(e)** An internal expenses-claim system must be live in ten weeks; the data model is simple, the team has a code generator and a component library, and two sub-teams can work in parallel.
→ **RAD.** Short timebox, modularisable, reuse available, committed users.

**(f)** A hospital wants a patient records system delivered so that admissions works from month three, billing from month six and analytics from month nine, because staff can only be trained in waves.
→ **Incremental.** Core product first, added function in planned increments.

**(g)** A team of 60 must build a large enterprise system, wants UML models, and needs an executable architecture agreed before the bulk of coding starts.
→ **Unified Process.** Use-case driven, architecture-centric, four phases.

blocks.title: Iterative, incremental and evolutionary are three different words
blocks.text:
**Incremental** = deliver the product in pieces; each increment adds *new* function and the first one is the core product.

**Iterative** = revisit and refine the *same* function repeatedly until it is right.

**Evolutionary** = the umbrella term for models that are iterative and let the product grow with changing requirements: prototyping, spiral, concurrent and component-based are all evolutionary. Waterfall and V are not. The incremental model is usually classified as evolutionary in Pressman and as its own category elsewhere — read the option list before deciding.

blocks.q: Which of the following is an umbrella activity rather than a generic framework activity?
blocks.exp: The five framework activities are Communication, Planning, Modeling, Construction and Deployment. Software configuration management is one of the eight umbrella activities that run across the entire life cycle, alongside risk management, SQA, technical reviews, measurement, reusability management, tracking and control, and work product preparation.

blocks.q: The distinguishing feature of the spiral model compared with the incremental model is that the spiral model
opts: delivers a core product in the first cycle
includes explicit risk analysis in every cycle
never returns to an earlier activity
blocks.exp: Both models iterate and both produce successively more complete versions, so options about delivering versions do not separate them. What only the spiral has is a dedicated risk-analysis region traversed on every circuit, which is why it is described as risk-driven and is recommended for large, high-risk systems. Formal specification belongs to the formal methods model.

blocks.q: In the Unified Process, an executable architectural baseline is produced during
blocks.exp: Inception establishes the business case and rough scope. Elaboration refines the use cases and delivers an executable architectural baseline — a running skeleton that proves the architecture. Construction then fills in the remaining components, and Transition handles beta release and deployment.

tricks.title: Match models by the one word in the stem
tricks.body: Exam stems are keyed to a single give-away: *risk* → spiral; *60 to 90 days* or *code generation* → RAD; *core product first* → incremental; *customer cannot state requirements* → prototyping; *mathematically verified / safety-critical* → formal methods; *crosscutting concern* → AOSD; *use-case driven, architecture-centric* → Unified Process; *COTS* → component-based. Read for that word before reading the options.

tricks.title: Five framework activities, eight umbrella activities
tricks.body: If the count in an option list is five, it is the framework list; if it is eight, it is the umbrella list. Any list of five that contains *testing* or *maintenance* as a separate item is wrong, because testing sits inside Construction.

tricks.title: Left arm meets right arm in the V-model
tricks.body: Pair the V-model levels from the outside in: requirements↔acceptance, system design↔system test, component design↔integration test, module design↔unit test. The outermost pair is always the customer-facing one.

tricks.title: Process pattern types scale by scope
tricks.body: Task ⊂ Stage ⊂ Phase. A pattern named after one activity (Communication) is a stage pattern; one named after a whole model (SpiralModel) is a phase pattern; one named after a single action (TechnicalReview) is a task pattern.

tricks.title: CMMI level 3 is where the process becomes organisational
tricks.body: Levels 1 and 2 are about individual projects; level 3 (Defined) is the first level with a single organisation-wide standard process; 4 adds statistics; 5 adds continuous improvement. If a question mentions statistical control, the answer is 4, not 5.

traps.title: Waterfall's problem is not that it has phases
traps.body: Every model has phases. Waterfall's specific faults are that it demands all requirements up front, that real projects do not progress strictly sequentially, and that no working program exists until very late in the schedule. Options that criticise waterfall for 'lacking documentation' or 'skipping design' are inverted.

traps.title: Unsafe to assume prototyping means throwaway
traps.body: Prototyping has two flavours. A throwaway prototype is built quickly and discarded; an evolutionary prototype becomes the product and must be built to production quality. Questions that describe a prototype being delivered to the customer are testing whether you know the second kind exists.

traps.title: RAD is incremental, not a form of waterfall
traps.body: RAD applies a compressed linear sequence to each parallel scope, but the overall model is incremental with parallel teams and a hard timebox. It is also not suitable for high technical risk — that is the spiral's territory.

traps.title: The spiral does not stop at delivery
traps.body: Unlike waterfall, the spiral model is described as applying throughout the life of the software: circuits continue for enhancement and maintenance. An option saying the spiral 'terminates when the software is delivered' is false.

topics.title: Agile Process Models
topics.summary: The Agile Manifesto's four values and twelve principles, XP's practices, Scrum's roles, artefacts and timeboxes, and the ASD, DSDM, FDD, Crystal, Lean, Kanban and web engineering variants.

blocks.text:
## What agility actually claims

Agility is not speed and it is not the absence of process. It is **effective response to change** at an economically acceptable cost. The classical models assume that the cost of changing a requirement rises steeply with time, so they push hard to freeze requirements early. Agile methods attack the assumption instead: by keeping increments tiny, the design simple, the tests automated and the customer in the room, they try to flatten that cost-of-change curve so that late change is affordable.

The practical consequences are always the same four: **short increments**, **working software as the measure of progress**, **the customer inside the team**, and **self-organising teams**. Everything below is a different arrangement of those four.

## The Agile Manifesto — four values

Signed at Snowbird, Utah in **2001** by seventeen practitioners. The wording matters because questions quote it:

> We are uncovering better ways of developing software by doing it and helping others do it. Through this work we have come to value:
> 1. **Individuals and interactions** over processes and tools
> 2. **Working software** over comprehensive documentation
> 3. **Customer collaboration** over contract negotiation
> 4. **Responding to change** over following a plan
>
> That is, while there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more.

The final sentence is the part candidates forget. The manifesto does **not** say documentation, tools, contracts and plans are worthless — it says they are the lesser of two goods.

## The twelve principles

Stated compactly, in the manifesto's own order:

1. Satisfy the customer through **early and continuous delivery** of valuable software.
2. **Welcome changing requirements**, even late in development.
3. Deliver working software **frequently** — weeks rather than months, preferring the shorter timescale.
4. Business people and developers must **work together daily**.
5. Build projects around **motivated individuals**; give them the environment and support they need and trust them.
6. **Face-to-face conversation** is the most efficient and effective method of conveying information within a team.
7. **Working software is the primary measure of progress.**
8. Promote **sustainable development** — sponsors, developers and users should be able to maintain a constant pace indefinitely.
9. Continuous attention to **technical excellence and good design** enhances agility.
10. **Simplicity** — the art of maximising the work not done — is essential.
11. The best architectures, requirements and designs emerge from **self-organising teams**.
12. At regular intervals the team **reflects** on how to become more effective and tunes its behaviour accordingly.

Principles 7 and 10 are the two most quoted. Principle 12 is the one Scrum implements as the retrospective.

## Extreme Programming (XP)

Kent Beck's method, the most widely used agile process. It rests on five **values**: **communication, simplicity, feedback, courage** and **respect**. Its process is four activities that cycle continuously.

**Planning.** Starts with *listening*, which produces **user stories** written on cards by the customer. Each story gets a **value** (priority) from the customer and a **cost** in development weeks from the team. A story costing more than three weeks is split. The team measures **project velocity** — the number of story points delivered in the first release — and uses it to estimate delivery dates and to cap the stories committed to in subsequent releases. The customer can add, change, split or reprioritise stories at any release boundary.

**Design.** Rigorously follows **KISS** — keep it simple. No extra functionality is designed in for tomorrow. **CRC cards** (Class-Responsibility-Collaborator) are the only design notation normally used. When a difficult design problem appears, the team builds a **spike solution**: a throwaway prototype of just that problem. **Refactoring** is a continuous design activity, not a clean-up phase: improve internal structure without changing external behaviour.

**Coding.** Before writing a story's code, write the **unit tests** for it — test-first development. Code is written in **pairs** at one workstation, providing real-time review. **Continuous integration**: pairs integrate their work as soon as it is ready, often several times a day, which avoids the compatibility and interfacing problems of a big-bang integration. **Collective ownership** means any pair may change any code.

**Testing.** Unit tests are collected into a **universal testing suite** that is run automatically on every integration, giving continuous regression testing. **Acceptance tests** (also called *customer tests*) are specified by the customer from the user stories and check externally visible behaviour.

The commonly examined list of **twelve XP practices** is: the planning game, small releases, metaphor, simple design, testing, refactoring, pair programming, collective ownership, continuous integration, 40-hour week (sustainable pace), on-site customer, coding standards.

**Industrial XP (IXP)** extends XP for larger organisations with readiness assessment, a project community, project chartering, test-driven management, retrospectives and continuous learning.

## Scrum

The framework by Schwaber and Beedle. Scrum is deliberately small: three roles, three artefacts, five events.

**Roles.** The **Product Owner** owns the product backlog, maximises value, and is a single person, not a committee. The **Scrum Master** is a servant-leader who removes impediments and protects the team from interruption; he or she is not a project manager and does not assign work. The **Development Team** is cross-functional, self-organising, and conventionally **3 to 9 members**.

**Artefacts.** The **Product Backlog** is the ordered list of everything that might be needed, owned by the Product Owner and continuously refined. The **Sprint Backlog** is the set of items selected for the current sprint plus the plan for delivering them, owned by the team. The **Increment** is the sum of all completed backlog items at the end of the sprint, which must meet the **Definition of Done** and be potentially releasable. Progress is commonly tracked on a **burndown chart** — remaining work on the vertical axis against time.

**Events and their timeboxes**, for a one-month sprint:

| Event | Timebox (1-month sprint) | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **The Sprint** | 1 month or less | the container for all other events |
| **Sprint Planning** | 8 hours | decide *what* can be delivered and *how* |
| **Daily Scrum** | **15 minutes**, same time and place every day | team re-plans the next 24 hours |
| **Sprint Review** | 4 hours | inspect the increment with stakeholders, adapt the backlog |
| **Sprint Retrospective** | 3 hours | inspect the *process*, plan improvements |

For shorter sprints the timeboxes are usually shorter in proportion — a two-week sprint takes 4 hours of planning, 2 hours of review and 1.5 hours of retrospective — but the **Daily Scrum stays at 15 minutes regardless of sprint length**. The three classic daily-scrum questions are: what did I do since the last meeting, what will I do before the next, and what is in my way. During a sprint no change may be made that endangers the sprint goal, and the sprint's scope is not expanded; only the Product Owner may cancel a sprint.

## The other agile methods

**ASD — Adaptive Software Development** (Jim Highsmith). Three phases with deliberately non-engineering names: **Speculation** (adaptive cycle planning — mission, constraints, release schedule), **Collaboration** (people work together to create; emphasis on trust and joint application development), **Learning** (focus groups, formal technical reviews, postmortems). The cycle is mission-driven, component-based, iterative, time-boxed, risk-driven and change-tolerant.

**DSDM — Dynamic Systems Development Method**. Built on the **Pareto principle**: deliver the 80% of the system that gives most of the value in 20% of the time, then iterate. Its five phases are **feasibility study, business study, functional model iteration, design and build iteration, implementation**. Requirements are prioritised with **MoSCoW**: **Must** have, **Should** have, **Could** have, **Won't** have this time. Nine principles, of which the most examined are that active user involvement is imperative, teams must be empowered to make decisions, and all changes during development are **reversible**. Time is fixed by timeboxing; scope flexes.

**FDD — Feature Driven Development** (Peter Coad, Jeff De Luca). A **feature** is a client-valued function expressible in the template *<action> the <result> <by|for|of|to> a(n) <object>*, for example "calculate the total of a sale". Any feature that would take more than **two weeks** is decomposed. Five activities: **develop an overall model, build a features list, plan by feature, design by feature, build by feature** — the first three are done once, the last two are the iterative engine. FDD scales better to large teams than XP because it keeps an overall object model and per-feature ownership.

**Crystal** (Alistair Cockburn and Jim Highsmith). Not one method but a **family**, chosen by two parameters: **team size**, which sets the colour, and **criticality**, which sets the ceremony. Colours run **Clear** (up to about 6–8 people) → **Yellow** (10–20) → **Orange** (20–40) → **Red** (40–80) and beyond. Criticality levels are the potential loss from a defect: **Comfort, Discretionary money, Essential money, Life**. Crystal's slogan is that a bigger or more critical project needs more method, and a small one needs very little.

**Lean software development**. Mary and Tom Poppendieck's transfer of the Toyota Production System. Seven principles: **eliminate waste, build quality in, create knowledge (amplify learning), defer commitment (decide as late as possible), deliver fast, respect people, optimise the whole**. Waste in software includes partially done work, extra features, relearning, hand-offs, task switching, delays and defects.

**Kanban**. A pull-based flow method with no prescribed iterations, roles or estimates. Its core practices: **visualise the workflow** on a board of columns; **limit work in progress (WIP)** with an explicit number per column; **manage flow** by measuring lead and cycle time; **make process policies explicit**; **implement feedback loops**; **improve collaboratively and evolve experimentally**. Limiting WIP is the mechanism — Little's law, $\text{WIP} = \text{throughput} \times \text{cycle time}$, says that halving WIP at constant throughput halves cycle time. Scrum timeboxes work; Kanban limits it.

**Agile Modeling (AM)** (Scott Ambler) supplies modelling practice — model with a purpose, use multiple models, travel light, model in small increments — for teams that need architecture but not documents. **AUP (Agile Unified Process)** is "serial in the large, iterative in the small": the four UP phases overall, agile iterations inside, with disciplines of modelling, implementation, testing, deployment, configuration and project management, and environment management.

## Web engineering

A **WebApp** is not a conventional program and the process must account for it. Its distinguishing attributes: network intensiveness, **concurrency** of many users, **unpredictable load**, demands on performance and 24×7 availability, being **data- and content-driven**, **continuous evolution** (content updated hourly, not annually), **immediacy** of the delivery window (days or weeks), heightened **security** exposure, and the weight carried by **aesthetics**.

The WebE process framework reuses the generic activities but specialises the content: **Communication** becomes *formulation* and negotiation of scope; **Planning** is a lightweight increment plan; **Modeling** produces five design models — **content design, aesthetic design, interface design, navigation design and architecture design**, plus component design; **Construction** uses generation tools and continuous testing; **Deployment** is a release into a live environment with immediate feedback. WebApp testing adds **content testing, navigation testing, configuration testing (browser/OS matrix), compatibility, usability, performance and security testing**. Incremental and agile processes dominate because the immediacy attribute forbids a long linear front end.

blocks.title: Worked example — sizing a Scrum sprint from velocity
blocks.text:
A team runs two-week sprints. Their last four sprints completed 26, 31, 29 and 34 story points. The product backlog, in priority order, is:

| Item | Points |
|---|---|
| A | 8 |
| B | 13 |
| C | 5 |
| D | 8 |
| E | 3 |
| F | 13 |

**Average velocity** $= (26 + 31 + 29 + 34)/4 = 120/4 = 30$ points per sprint.

**Sprint forecast.** Taking items strictly in backlog order until the velocity is reached: A (8) → running total 8; B (13) → 21; C (5) → 26; D (8) → 34, which exceeds 30. Since D does not fit, the team takes A, B, C for 26 points and may pull E (3) to reach **29 points**, leaving D and F.

**Release forecast.** Total remaining backlog $= 8+13+5+8+3+13 = 50$ points. At a velocity of 30, the number of sprints needed is $\lceil 50/30 \rceil = 2$ sprints, i.e. **4 weeks**.

**Timeboxes for this two-week sprint**, scaling the one-month figures by half: Sprint Planning 4 hours, Sprint Review 2 hours, Sprint Retrospective 1.5 hours, and the **Daily Scrum still 15 minutes** — it never scales.

Note what is *not* done: the team does not take D "because it is only 8 points over" and does not add scope mid-sprint. Velocity is a forecast, not a target, and the sprint scope is fixed once the sprint starts.

blocks.title: Which agile method owns which term
blocks.text:
A single-word lookup that answers most match-the-list questions.

| Term | Method |
|---|---|
| User story, spike solution, CRC cards, pair programming, refactoring | **XP** |
| Sprint, backlog, Scrum Master, burndown, retrospective | **Scrum** |
| Speculation, Collaboration, Learning | **ASD** |
| MoSCoW, timebox, 80/20, feasibility and business study | **DSDM** |
| Feature, "design by feature", overall object model | **FDD** |
| Clear / Yellow / Orange / Red, criticality levels | **Crystal** |
| Eliminate waste, defer commitment, optimise the whole | **Lean** |
| WIP limit, pull system, cumulative flow diagram | **Kanban** |

blocks.q: The timebox for the Daily Scrum in a two-week sprint is
opts: proportional to sprint length, so 7.5 minutes
blocks.exp: Sprint Planning, Review and Retrospective are usually scaled down for shorter sprints (4 hours, 2 hours and 1.5 hours respectively for a two-week sprint), but the Daily Scrum is fixed at 15 minutes for every sprint length. It is a re-planning meeting for the next 24 hours, and 24 hours does not change with sprint length.

blocks.q: Which pairing of agile method and concept is INCORRECT?
blocks.exp: Sprint backlog is a Scrum artefact, not an XP one; XP's planning unit is the user story and its release plan. DSDM does use MoSCoW (Must, Should, Could, Won't), FDD's five activities do include design by feature and build by feature, and Crystal selects a family member using team size and criticality (Comfort, Discretionary money, Essential money, Life).

blocks.q: According to the Agile Manifesto, which statement is correct?
opts: Documentation has no value in agile projects
Following a plan is preferred to responding to change
Processes and tools are valued more than individuals and interactions
Working software is valued more than comprehensive documentation, but documentation still has value
blocks.exp: Each of the four values is a comparison, and the manifesto closes by stating explicitly that while there is value in the items on the right, the items on the left are valued more. So documentation, plans, contracts and tools are not rejected — they are ranked lower than working software, responsiveness, collaboration and people.

tricks.title: Counts pin the method
tricks.body: Agile Manifesto: 4 values, 12 principles, 2001, 17 signatories. XP: 5 values, 4 activities, 12 practices. Scrum: 3 roles, 3 artefacts, 5 events. ASD: 3 phases. DSDM: 5 phases, 9 principles. FDD: 5 activities. Lean: 7 principles. If an option's count is wrong the option is wrong, without reading further.

tricks.title: Velocity divides, it does not multiply
tricks.body: For 'how many sprints to finish the backlog', compute total points divided by average velocity and round up. For 'what fits in this sprint', fill in strict priority order and stop at the first item that overflows — do not repack to maximise utilisation.

tricks.title: Stubs of the daily scrum
tricks.body: Daily Scrum = 15 minutes, everyone standing, same time and place, three questions, no problem-solving. Any option that gives it a variable duration or turns it into a status report to the Scrum Master is wrong.

tricks.title: XP's test-first order
tricks.body: In XP the unit tests are written before the code they test, and acceptance tests are derived from user stories by the customer. If a question asks what happens first in an XP coding episode, the answer is 'write the unit test', never 'write the code'.

tricks.title: Scrum Master is not a manager
tricks.body: When a question describes someone assigning tasks, estimating for the team, or committing scope on the team's behalf, that person is not playing the Scrum Master role as defined. The Scrum Master removes impediments and enforces the framework; the team self-organises; the Product Owner orders the backlog.

traps.title: Agile does not mean no documentation and no design
traps.body: Principle 9 explicitly demands continuous attention to technical excellence and good design, and the manifesto states the right-hand items still have value. The distinction is that documents are produced when they earn their keep, not on a schedule.

traps.title: Incremental delivery alone is not agility
traps.body: Delivering in increments is necessary but not sufficient. Agility requires responsiveness to change at acceptable cost — which needs the customer available, the tests automated and the design kept simple. A waterfall chopped into three deliveries is still a waterfall.

traps.title: Scrum has no architect, tester or analyst role
traps.body: Scrum defines exactly three accountabilities. The development team is cross-functional and contains whatever skills are needed, but Scrum names no sub-roles inside it. Options listing 'Project Manager' or 'Technical Lead' among Scrum roles are distractors.

traps.title: Kanban and Scrum limit different things
traps.body: Scrum limits time — a fixed-length sprint with a committed scope. Kanban limits work in progress — an explicit cap per column, with no iterations, no prescribed roles and no estimation required. Swapping the two is the standard distractor.

topics.title: Software Requirements
topics.summary: Functional and non-functional requirements, the seven requirements-engineering tasks, elicitation techniques, use cases and scenarios, analysis modelling, and the IEEE 830 SRS with its eight quality attributes.

blocks.text:
## What a requirement is, and why they go wrong

A **requirement** is a statement of a service the system must provide, or a constraint on it. Requirements sit at the point where the customer's world and the engineer's world meet, which is exactly why they are the largest single source of project failure: a fault injected in requirements is cheap to fix while it is still a sentence and ruinously expensive once it has propagated through design, code and tests. Boehm's classic figure is that the relative cost of correcting an error rises roughly by an order of magnitude with each phase it survives.

Requirements come in two kinds and the distinction is asked almost every year.

**Functional requirements** say *what the system does*: the services, the inputs it accepts, the outputs it produces, how it behaves in particular situations, and what it must not do. "The system shall generate a monthly interest statement for every active account on the first working day of the month" is functional.

**Non-functional requirements (NFRs)** constrain *how well* the system does it, or constrain the development process or the product's environment. "Ninety-five per cent of statement generations shall complete within two seconds" is non-functional. NFRs are usually harder to state, harder to verify, and more likely to be the reason a delivered system is rejected, because a single unmet NFR can make the whole system unusable while a single missing function merely reduces its scope.

Sommerville's standard classification of NFRs:

| Class | Sub-types | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Product requirements** | usability, efficiency (performance, space), reliability, portability, security | response time, memory footprint, MTBF |
| **Organisational requirements** | environmental, operational, development (process, standards) | must use the company's Java coding standard; must be delivered as a Docker image |
| **External requirements** | regulatory, ethical, legislative (accounting, safety/security), interoperability | must comply with data-protection law; must exchange HL7 messages |

A third category sometimes examined is **domain requirements** — constraints coming from the application domain itself, which may be functional or non-functional and are often left implicit by domain experts, making them a notorious source of omissions.

## Requirements engineering: the seven tasks

Pressman splits requirements engineering into seven tasks. The order is examinable.

1. **Inception** — establish a basic understanding of the problem, who wants it, the nature of the solution, and the first contact between stakeholders and the team. Ask context-free questions: who is behind the request, who will use it, what is the economic benefit, is there another source.
2. **Elicitation** — draw the requirements out of the stakeholders.
3. **Elaboration** — expand and refine what was elicited into an analysis model: user scenarios, extracted analysis classes, attributes, services, relationships.
4. **Negotiation** — reconcile conflicts. Stakeholders ask for more than can be built; requirements are ranked, risk-assessed and traded until a realistic set is agreed.
5. **Specification** — produce the deliverable: a written document, a set of models, a formal mathematical specification, a prototype, or any combination. For large systems this is the **SRS**.
6. **Validation** — review the specification for quality: are the requirements unambiguous, consistent, testable, complete, and are the omissions and inconsistencies found before design begins? The primary mechanism is the **formal technical review**.
7. **Requirements management** — track, trace and control requirements as they change through the life of the project, using traceability tables (features, source, dependency, subsystem, interface).

Christel and Kang's classification of why elicitation is hard is worth memorising: **problems of scope** (boundary ill-defined, unnecessary technical detail), **problems of understanding** (stakeholders unsure what they need, poor communication, ambiguous language, conflicting views), and **problems of volatility** (requirements change over time).

## Elicitation techniques

| Technique | How it works | Best when |
|---|---|---|
| **Interviews** | structured (fixed agenda) or unstructured (open exploration) | small stakeholder set; deep understanding needed |
| **Questionnaires** | fixed questions to many respondents | many geographically spread users; statistical picture wanted |
| **FAST / JAD** | Facilitated Application Specification Technique: a facilitated joint meeting of customers and developers, neutral site, agenda, lists of objects, services, constraints and performance criteria produced and consolidated | requirements span several business groups |
| **Brainstorming** | idea generation without criticism, then consolidation | early inception; innovative products |
| **Prototyping** | show something and observe the reaction | customer cannot articulate the requirement |
| **Observation / ethnography** | watch users work in their real setting | tacit knowledge; existing manual process |
| **Document analysis** | study forms, manuals, regulations, existing code | replacing a legacy system |
| **Use cases and scenarios** | narrate concrete interactions | validating with non-technical stakeholders |
| **QFD — Quality Function Deployment** | translate customer needs into technical requirements; ranks requirements by customer value | when priorities must be quantified |
| **Viewpoint-oriented** | collect requirements per stakeholder class, then reconcile | conflicting stakeholder groups |

**QFD** classifies requirements into three bands that examiners like: **normal requirements** (objectives stated by the customer; satisfaction is proportional to how well they are met), **expected requirements** (so fundamental the customer does not mention them — the system must not crash, the interface must be usable), and **exciting requirements** (features beyond expectation that delight when present).

## Use cases and scenarios

A **use case** is a description of a set of interactions between the system and one or more **actors**, written from the actor's point of view, that delivers an observable result of value. To write one you need: the **actor** (a role, not a person — a primary actor drives the system directly, a secondary actor supports it), the **goal**, the **preconditions**, the **main flow** (also called the primary scenario or happy path), the **alternative flows**, the **exception flows**, and the **postconditions**.

A **scenario** is one concrete path through a use case. One use case therefore contains many scenarios: exactly one primary scenario and any number of alternative and exception scenarios.

Relationships between use cases in UML:

- **<<include>>** — the base use case *always* uses the included one; the included behaviour is factored out because it is common. "Withdraw cash" includes "Authenticate user".
- **<<extend>>** — the extending use case *conditionally* adds behaviour at a defined extension point. "Withdraw cash" is extended by "Print receipt".
- **Generalisation** — one use case (or actor) is a specialisation of another.

The direction of the arrow is the standard trap: for both include and extend the arrow points *from* the use case that declares the relationship *to* the other one, which means the extend arrow points from the extension to the base — the opposite of the include arrow's apparent direction of flow.

## Analysis modelling

The analysis model bridges the system description and the design model. Pressman groups its elements into four kinds:

| Element | Notation | What it captures |
|---|---|---|
| **Scenario-based** | use case diagrams, activity diagrams, swimlane diagrams | the system from the user's viewpoint |
| **Class-based** | class diagrams, CRC cards, collaboration diagrams | objects, attributes, operations, relationships |
| **Flow-oriented** | data flow diagrams, control flow diagrams, process specifications (PSPEC) | how data is transformed as it moves |
| **Behavioural** | state diagrams, sequence diagrams | how the system reacts to events |

**Data flow diagrams** deserve their own rules. Notation: a circle (bubble) is a process, an arrow a data flow, a double line (or open rectangle) a data store, a rectangle an external entity. The **level 0 DFD is the context diagram** and contains exactly **one** bubble representing the entire system plus all external entities. Refining a bubble into a lower-level DFD is **levelling**; the rule that the inputs and outputs of the refined diagram must match those of the parent bubble is **balancing**. Data stores appear only from level 1 downwards, and a DFD shows no control flow, no decisions and no loops — that is a flowchart's job, and confusing the two is a standard distractor.

**Data dictionary** entries define every flow and store using the notation `=` (is composed of), `+` (and), `[a|b]` (either-or), `{x}` (iteration), `(x)` (optional).

**Entity-relationship diagrams** carry the data model: entities, attributes, relationships and cardinality/modality. **State diagrams** carry the behavioural model, with states as rounded rectangles and transitions labelled *event [guard] / action*.

## The SRS and IEEE 830

The **Software Requirements Specification** is the contract: it states what the system will do, is agreed by customer and supplier, and becomes the baseline against which design is verified and acceptance tests are written. **IEEE Std 830-1998** gives the canonical structure:

**1. Introduction**
  1.1 Purpose
  1.2 Scope
  1.3 Definitions, acronyms and abbreviations
  1.4 References
  1.5 Overview

**2. Overall description**
  2.1 Product perspective (interfaces, memory, operations, site adaptation)
  2.2 Product functions
  2.3 User characteristics
  2.4 Constraints
  2.5 Assumptions and dependencies
  2.6 Apportioning of requirements

**3. Specific requirements**
  external interface requirements; functional requirements; performance requirements; logical database requirements; design constraints; software system attributes (reliability, availability, security, maintainability, portability)

**Appendixes. Index.**

Note the split that questions exploit: section 2 is a **general, non-binding overview for the reader**, while section 3 contains the **detailed, verifiable requirements that developers and testers actually work from**. Section 2 does not state requirements in a testable form; section 3 does.

### The eight qualities of a good SRS

IEEE 830 says an SRS should be:

1. **Correct** — every requirement stated is one the system must meet.
2. **Unambiguous** — every requirement has exactly one interpretation.
3. **Complete** — all significant requirements, all responses to all inputs, all figures and definitions labelled; no "to be determined" left.
4. **Consistent** — no requirement conflicts with another (in terminology, in logic, or in characteristics).
5. **Ranked for importance and/or stability** — each requirement marked essential/conditional/optional and marked by how likely it is to change.
6. **Verifiable** — a finite, cost-effective process exists to check the product meets it. "The system shall be user-friendly" is not verifiable; "a trained operator shall complete a booking in under 90 seconds" is.
7. **Modifiable** — well organised, with a table of contents, index and cross-references, and no redundancy, so that a change can be made cleanly.
8. **Traceable** — backward traceable to the source that produced it, and forward traceable to the design and code elements that implement it.

Some textbooks add *usable during operation and maintenance* as a ninth. The list of eight above is the one to reproduce.

blocks.title: Worked example — turning a vague statement into good requirements
blocks.text:
A library customer says: *"The system should let members reserve books, and it must be fast and secure."*

**Step 1 — separate functional from non-functional.**
- Functional kernel: "let members reserve books."
- Non-functional kernel: "fast", "secure".

**Step 2 — make the functional part complete.** A reserve-book service needs its inputs, outputs, preconditions and exception behaviour spelled out:

> **FR-12.** The system shall allow an authenticated member with fewer than five active reservations to place a reservation on any title that has no available copy. On success the system shall record the reservation with a timestamp and return the member's position in the queue. If the member already has five active reservations, the system shall reject the request and display "Reservation limit reached".

That single sentence fixes the actor, the precondition, the trigger, the output and one exception path.

**Step 3 — make the non-functional parts verifiable.** "Fast" and "secure" are unverifiable as written, violating quality 6.

> **NFR-4 (performance).** Under a load of 200 concurrent users, 95% of reservation requests shall receive a response within 2 seconds and 100% within 5 seconds, measured at the web tier.
>
> **NFR-5 (security).** Member passwords shall be stored only as salted hashes using an algorithm on the approved list in Appendix B. Three consecutive failed logins shall lock the account for 15 minutes.

**Step 4 — check against the qualities.** FR-12 is unambiguous (one reading), verifiable (a test can place six reservations), traceable (it can be labelled as arising from stakeholder request SR-3 and linked forward to the design class `ReservationManager`), and ranked (mark it *essential*, stability *high*). NFR-4 is now verifiable because it names the load, the percentile, the threshold and the measurement point — any one of those four missing makes it untestable again.

**Step 5 — spot what is still missing.** Nothing says what happens when a reserved copy becomes available, how long the member has to collect it, or whether reservations expire. That is an incompleteness, and finding it is exactly the job of requirements **validation** by formal technical review.

blocks.title: Which quality is being violated?
blocks.text:
Questions give one bad requirement and ask which SRS property it breaks. Use these signatures.

| Bad requirement | Violated quality |
|---|---|
| "The interface shall be user-friendly." | **Verifiable** (also unambiguous) |
| "Response time shall be fast" in §3 and "under 1 s" in §5 | **Consistent** |
| "The system shall support many users." | **Unambiguous** |
| No statement of what happens on invalid input | **Complete** |
| No labels or IDs on requirements, heavy redundancy | **Modifiable** |
| No link from a requirement back to who asked for it | **Traceable** |
| Every requirement written as equally mandatory | **Ranked for importance** |

blocks.q: "The system shall encrypt all stored customer records using AES-256." This requirement is best classified as
blocks.exp: It constrains a quality of the product — its security — rather than naming a service the system delivers to a user, so it is non-functional, and within Sommerville's classification it is a product requirement (the security sub-type). It would be an external requirement only if the SRS derived it from a named law or standard rather than from the product's own quality goals.

blocks.q: In a level 0 data flow diagram, the number of processes shown is
opts: as many as the analyst chooses
blocks.exp: The level 0 DFD is the context diagram: the entire system is drawn as a single bubble, surrounded by the external entities and the flows between them and the system. Decomposition into multiple processes begins at level 1, and the levelling must be balanced — the level 1 diagram's net inputs and outputs must match the single level 0 bubble's.

blocks.q: An SRS states requirement R7 in section 3 and repeats the same rule in different words in section 5, where the two versions disagree about a threshold. Which SRS quality is primarily violated?
blocks.exp: Two statements in the same document that cannot both be satisfied is precisely an internal inconsistency. The redundancy also hurts modifiability, since a change must be made in two places, but the direct and primary violation named by IEEE 830 for conflicting requirements is consistency.

tricks.title: The 'how well' test separates FR from NFR
tricks.body: Ask whether the sentence answers *what does it do* or *how well / under what constraint does it do it*. Performance, security, availability, usability, portability, standards compliance and legal conformance are always non-functional, even when they mention a specific function.

tricks.title: Seven RE tasks in order: I-E-E-N-S-V-M
tricks.body: Inception, Elicitation, Elaboration, Negotiation, Specification, Validation, Management. Note that Negotiation comes before Specification — you agree the set, then write it down — and Management is not a phase but runs throughout.

tricks.title: Verifiability is the quality most often tested
tricks.body: When asked what is wrong with a requirement, look first for an adjective with no number attached: fast, reliable, robust, user-friendly, efficient, secure, easy. Each of those makes the requirement unverifiable and usually ambiguous as well.

tricks.title: Include is mandatory, extend is optional
tricks.body: If the base use case cannot complete without the other, it is include. If the other adds behaviour only in certain circumstances at a named extension point, it is extend. Read the words 'always' and 'optionally' in the stem.

tricks.title: IEEE 830 section 2 versus section 3
tricks.body: Anything described as a background, perspective, user characteristic, assumption or constraint overview belongs in section 2 (Overall description). Anything stated as a numbered, testable shall-statement belongs in section 3 (Specific requirements).

traps.title: A DFD is not a flowchart
traps.body: A DFD shows data transformation, not control. It has no decision diamonds, no loops, no sequencing and no indication of when a process runs — only that data arriving causes data to leave. Options that credit a DFD with showing conditions or order of execution are wrong.

traps.title: Validation and verification of requirements are different questions
traps.body: Requirements validation asks whether the SRS describes the system the customer wants; requirements verification asks whether the SRS is internally well formed. In the seven-task list the named activity is validation, and its main technique is the formal technical review, not testing — there is no code yet.

traps.title: A scenario is not a use case
traps.body: A use case is the whole set of interaction paths for a goal; a scenario is one specific path through it. A question saying 'each use case corresponds to exactly one scenario' is false: there is one primary scenario plus alternative and exception scenarios.

traps.title: Completeness does not mean 'long'
traps.body: IEEE 830 completeness means every significant requirement is present, every response to every class of input in every situation is defined, and every figure and term is labelled and defined — with no 'TBD' left. A thick document full of prose can still be incomplete, and a short one with full input-response coverage can be complete.

topics.title: Software Design
topics.summary: Design concepts and the modularity trade-off, the complete cohesion and coupling ladders in order, architectural styles, and data, architectural, interface and component-level design.

blocks.text:
## From analysis model to design model

Analysis says *what*; design says *how*. Design takes the analysis model and produces four things, which are also the four **levels of design**:

| Level | Produces | From |
|---|---|---|
| **Data / class design** | data structures and design classes | class-based analysis elements, ERD |
| **Architectural design** | the relationship among the major structural elements | class-based and flow-oriented elements |
| **Interface design** | how the software communicates with users, other systems and itself | scenario-based and behavioural elements |
| **Component-level design** | procedural descriptions of each component | all of the above, refined |

Design quality is judged by three rules (the classic "goals of design"): the design must implement all explicit requirements and all implicit ones the customer expects; it must be readable and understandable by those who will code, test and maintain it; and it must give a complete picture of the data, function and behaviour domains from an implementation perspective.

## The design concepts

These are the intellectual tools the designer uses. Pressman's list, with what each is actually for:

- **Abstraction** — describe a solution at a level of detail appropriate to the problem. A **procedural abstraction** names a sequence of instructions with a single function ("open the door"); a **data abstraction** names a collection of data ("door" with attributes type, weight, dimensions). Design proceeds from high to low abstraction.
- **Architecture** — the overall structure: the components, their externally visible properties, and their relationships. It is not the source code; it is the framework the code hangs on.
- **Patterns** — named, reusable solutions to recurring design problems, each carrying the context in which it applies and the consequences of using it.
- **Separation of concerns** — divide a problem into pieces that can be solved independently. The justification is that the perceived complexity of two sub-problems solved separately is less than the complexity of solving them together: if $p_1$ and $p_2$ are problems with perceived complexity $C(p_1) > C(p_2)$, then $E(p_1) > E(p_2)$ for the effort, and crucially $C(p_1 + p_2) > C(p_1) + C(p_2)$.
- **Modularity** — the practical form of separation of concerns: software divided into named, addressable components that can be developed and tested independently.
- **Information hiding** (Parnas) — each module hides its design decisions from all others; interfaces reveal only what is necessary. The benefit is that when a hidden decision changes, only that module changes, so errors do not propagate. Information hiding is the *reason* modular designs are maintainable.
- **Functional independence** — each module addresses one sub-function and has simple interfaces. Measured by **cohesion** and **coupling**.
- **Refinement** (Wirth's stepwise refinement) — elaborate a statement of function through successive levels of detail. Refinement and abstraction are complementary: abstraction suppresses detail, refinement reveals it.
- **Aspects** — a representation of a crosscutting concern, needed when a requirement cannot be satisfied without cutting across several modules.
- **Refactoring** — reorganising a design or code to improve internal structure without changing external behaviour.
- **Design classes** — five types refine the analysis classes: user interface, business domain, process, persistent, and system classes.

### The modularity trade-off

Splitting into more modules reduces the effort per module, but integration effort — the cost of the interfaces between them — grows with the number of modules. The total cost is the sum of these two opposing curves, so it has a minimum:

$$\text{Cost}_{\text{total}}(m) = \text{Cost}_{\text{modules}}(m) + \text{Cost}_{\text{interface}}(m)$$

The region around that minimum is the **region of minimum cost**, and the number of modules there is often labelled $M$. Below it the design is **undermodular** (a few huge modules); above it, **overmodular** (integration overhead swamps the benefit). The honest answer to "how many modules?" is that there is no formula — but the shape of the curve is examined, and the expected answer to "does modularity always reduce cost?" is **no**.

## Cohesion — the seven levels, worst to best

**Cohesion** measures how strongly the elements *inside* one module belong together. High cohesion is desired. The ladder is asked almost every year, usually as "arrange in increasing order of cohesion" or "which is the strongest/weakest form".

| Rank | Level | The elements are grouped because... | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (worst) | **Coincidental** | no reason at all; arbitrary grouping | a `Utils` module holding `printBanner`, `sortArray` and `openSocket` |
| 2 | **Logical** | they are the same *kind* of thing, with a flag selecting which one runs | one `handleIO(type)` routine that reads a tape, a disk or a keyboard according to `type` |
| 3 | **Temporal** | they all happen at the same *time* | `initialise()` that opens files, zeroes counters and sets the clock |
| 4 | **Procedural** | they must execute in a particular *order* | `readRecord(); validate(); writeLog()` where the only link is sequence |
| 5 | **Communicational** | they all operate on the *same data* | a module that computes the total, the mean and the maximum of the same array |
| 6 | **Sequential** | the *output of one is the input of the next* | `parse()` feeding `evaluate()` feeding `format()` |
| 7 (best) | **Functional** | they all contribute to exactly *one* well-defined task | `computeSquareRoot(x)` |

Remember the ladder as **Co-Lo-Te-Pro-Com-Se-Fun**. Object-oriented treatments sometimes insert **informational cohesion** (a module with several entry points, each performing one function, all sharing one data structure — essentially an abstract data type) between sequential and functional, and Pressman's component-level list uses the shorter set *functional, layer, communicational*. If an option list has eight entries, informational is the extra one.

The two most confused neighbours are **procedural** and **sequential**. Both involve order. The test is: does data flow from one element to the next? If the second element consumes what the first produced, it is sequential; if they merely have to run in that order but pass nothing, it is procedural. Similarly **communicational** and **sequential** both involve shared data — but in communicational the elements all touch the same data independently, while in sequential they form a chain.

## Coupling — the six levels, worst to best

**Coupling** measures the interdependence *between* modules. Low coupling is desired.

| Rank | Level | Nature of the dependency | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (worst) | **Content** (pathological) | one module modifies or relies on the internal workings of another — branches into its middle, changes its local data | `goto` into another routine's body; altering another module's local variable |
| 2 | **Common** (global) | two modules share global data | both read and write a global `config` record |
| 3 | **External** | modules share an externally imposed item — a device, a protocol, a file format | two modules both bound to the same communication protocol |
| 4 | **Control** | one module passes a flag that dictates the other's internal logic | `process(data, mode)` where `mode` selects which branch runs inside |
| 5 | **Stamp** (data-structured) | modules share a composite data structure but each uses only part of it | passing a whole `Employee` record when only the salary is needed |
| 6 (best) | **Data** | modules communicate only through simple parameters, each of which is used | `computeTax(income, rate)` |

Remember **Content-Common-External-Control-Stamp-Data**. Beyond data coupling some texts list **message coupling** (communication via parameterless messages or events, as in pure object-oriented systems) and **no coupling** as still looser, and place **subclass coupling** and **temporal coupling** among the object-oriented varieties. The six above are the classical Stevens–Myers–Constantine set.

Content and common are the pair that kill maintainability, because a change in one module silently breaks another. Control coupling is the one candidates misclassify: the giveaway is a parameter that is a *switch* rather than *data*. Stamp versus data is decided by whether the argument is a composite structure of which only part is used.

### Using both together

Functional independence is high cohesion **and** low coupling simultaneously. An exam favourite is: which combination is best? **High cohesion, low coupling.** And which module has the best design characteristics? The one whose elements all serve one purpose and which talks to its neighbours only through simple parameters.

## Architectural styles

An **architectural style** names a family of systems with a shared structural organisation. It defines a set of component types, a set of connectors, constraints on how they may be combined, and a semantic model.

| Style | Organisation | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **Data-centred** (repository, blackboard) | a central data store that clients access; in the blackboard variant the store notifies clients of changes | database applications, AI problem solvers |
| **Data-flow** (batch sequential, **pipe and filter**) | a chain of filters, each transforming its input stream; connectors are pipes | compilers, Unix shells, signal processing |
| **Call and return** | main program/subprogram hierarchy or remote procedure call; control flows down and returns | classic procedural systems |
| **Layered** | a hierarchy of layers, each using only the layer below; inner layers hold core functionality, outer layers interface with users | operating systems, network stacks |
| **Object-oriented** | components encapsulate data and the operations on it; interaction by message passing | most modern business systems |

Related, commonly examined organisations: **client-server** (two-tier and three-tier: presentation, application logic, data), **MVC** (Model holds data and business rules, View renders, Controller interprets user input and selects the model behaviour), **broker** (a middleware component decouples clients and servers, as in CORBA), **publish-subscribe / event-driven**, and **microkernel**.

Architectural design also uses **archetypes** (abstractions central to the domain), **architectural context diagrams**, and evaluation methods such as **ATAM** (Architecture Trade-off Analysis Method).

### Structured design: DFD to structure chart

Classical structured design maps an analysis DFD onto a program structure chart:

- **Transform mapping** — used when the DFD shows a clear *incoming flow* (afferent), a *central transform*, and an *outgoing flow* (efferent). The flow boundaries are drawn, the chart is factored into an input controller, a transform controller and an output controller under a top-level module, then refined.
- **Transaction mapping** — used when a single data item, a **transaction**, triggers one of several possible action paths. The structure chart gets a *transaction centre* (dispatcher) with one branch per action path.

Structure-chart vocabulary: **fan-out** is the number of modules directly controlled by a module; **fan-in** is the number of modules that control it; **depth** is the number of levels; **width** the maximum span at any level. The **scope of effect** of a decision (the modules affected by it) should lie **within the scope of control** of the module in which the decision is taken — a rule that shows up as a true/false statement.

## Interface and component-level design

**Interface design** covers the user interface, external interfaces to other systems, and internal interfaces between components. Theo Mandel's three **golden rules** are the examined part:

1. **Place the user in control** — interaction modes should not force the user down a path; provide undo; allow interruption; hide technical internals.
2. **Reduce the user's memory load** — set meaningful defaults, use recognisable shortcuts, disclose information progressively, make recent actions visible.
3. **Make the interface consistent** — consistent visual layout, consistent input mechanisms, consistent navigation; preserve context when moving between tasks.

The user-interface design process is itself spiral: *interface analysis and modelling* (user, task, environment analysis) → *interface design* → *interface construction/prototype* → *interface validation*.

**Component-level design** turns each architectural component into a procedural description. Its foundation is **structured programming**: only the three constructs **sequence, condition (if-then-else, case) and repetition (while, until)** are used, each with one entry and one exit, which guarantees the design is comprehensible and testable.

Three notations are available:

- **Graphical** — flowcharts, box (Nassi-Shneiderman/chapin) diagrams.
- **Tabular** — **decision tables**, which pair a set of conditions with the actions each combination triggers, and are the right choice when a component is a tangle of conditions.
- **Program design language (PDL)** — structured English, or "pseudocode": the control structures of a programming language with the descriptive freedom of prose.

**Object-oriented design** replaces procedural decomposition with class decomposition. Its concepts are **classes and objects, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, message passing** and **abstraction**. A design class comes in the five flavours listed earlier, and is refined until each class has a single, tight responsibility — the OO restatement of functional cohesion. Its structural principles are commonly examined as the **open-closed principle** (open for extension, closed for modification), the **Liskov substitution principle** (a subclass must be usable wherever its superclass is), **dependency inversion** (depend on abstractions, not concretions) and the **interface segregation principle**. The classic methodologies are **Booch**, **Rumbaugh's OMT** (object model, dynamic model, functional model), **Jacobson's OOSE** (use-case driven) and **Coad-Yourdon**, all of which converged into **UML**.

Design **patterns** are catalogued by the Gang of Four in three families: **creational** (Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype), **structural** (Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, Proxy) and **behavioural** (Observer, Strategy, Command, Iterator, State, Template Method, Visitor, Mediator, Memento, Chain of Responsibility, Interpreter) — 23 in all.

blocks.title: Worked example — classifying cohesion and coupling from code
Two ladders, memorised in one line each
blocks.text:
**Cohesion, worst → best (7):** **Co**incidental, **Lo**gical, **Te**mporal, **Pro**cedural, **Com**municational, **Se**quential, **Fun**ctional.
Read the initials as *"Co-Lo-Te-Pro-Com-Se-Fun"*.

**Coupling, worst → best (6):** **Co**ntent, **Co**mmon, **E**xternal, **C**ontrol, **S**tamp, **D**ata.
Read the initials as *"CoCECSD"*, or remember that the two worst both start with *Co* and the best is the simplest word, *Data*.

Both ladders are conventionally written worst-first. If a question says "increasing cohesion" it wants this order; if it says "decreasing cohesion" reverse it. Check which direction the stem asks for before matching.

blocks.q: Arrange the following in order of increasing cohesion: (i) Procedural (ii) Coincidental (iii) Sequential (iv) Temporal
blocks.exp: The ladder from weakest to strongest is coincidental, logical, temporal, procedural, communicational, sequential, functional. Taking only the four listed, that gives coincidental (weakest), then temporal, then procedural, then sequential (strongest) — option (ii), (iv), (i), (iii).

blocks.q: Module A passes module B a complete customer record, although B uses only the postcode field. The coupling between A and B is
blocks.exp: Stamp coupling is exactly this: a composite data structure is passed but the receiver uses only part of it, so B is exposed to changes in fields it never reads. Passing the postcode alone as a simple parameter would be data coupling, the loosest of the classical forms; control coupling needs a flag that directs B's internal logic, and common coupling needs shared global data.

blocks.q: Which statement about information hiding is correct?
opts: It requires each module to expose all of its data so that others can reuse it
It means design decisions inside a module are inaccessible to other modules, so changes do not propagate
It is a synonym for abstraction
It increases coupling to improve performance
blocks.exp: Parnas's principle is that each module conceals its design decisions behind an interface, so a change to a hidden decision is confined to that module and cannot ripple through the system. That is why it is the justification for modularity's maintainability benefits. Abstraction is a related but distinct concept: it suppresses detail at a level of description, whereas information hiding enforces inaccessibility.

tricks.title: The ladder order is worth more marks than the definitions
tricks.body: Three or four questions a year ask only for the order. Drill 'Co-Lo-Te-Pro-Com-Se-Fun' for cohesion and 'Content-Common-External-Control-Stamp-Data' for coupling until you can write both without thinking, then classify from the definitions only when the stem gives code.

tricks.title: Procedural vs sequential: does data flow?
tricks.body: Both imply an order of execution. If module element 2 consumes what element 1 produced, it is sequential (higher). If they just have to happen in that order but exchange nothing, it is procedural (lower).

tricks.title: A flag parameter is always control coupling
tricks.body: Any argument whose purpose is to select behaviour inside the callee — a mode, a type, a switch, a boolean that gates a branch — is control coupling, no matter how simple it looks. A flag that is merely stored or returned unexamined is data.

tricks.title: Cohesion is within, coupling is between
tricks.body: If the question describes what is inside one module, it is a cohesion question; if it describes how two modules talk, it is coupling. Candidates lose marks by reading a coupling stem and answering from the cohesion ladder.

tricks.title: Transform vs transaction mapping by DFD shape
tricks.body: If the DFD is a straight pipeline with an identifiable centre, use transform mapping. If one incoming item fans out to several mutually exclusive action paths, use transaction mapping and expect a dispatcher module in the structure chart.

traps.title: More modules is not always better
traps.body: The total cost curve is U-shaped: module cost falls with $m$ but interface cost rises, so beyond the region of minimum cost, adding modules increases total effort. 'Modularity always reduces development cost' is false.

traps.title: Coincidental cohesion is worst, functional is best — not the reverse
traps.body: Because coupling's best value is 'data' and cohesion's best is 'functional', candidates sometimes assume both ladders are printed best-first. Both are conventionally printed worst-first. Always check the direction word in the stem.

traps.title: Common coupling is not the worst
traps.body: Global data is bad but content coupling is worse, because a content-coupled module reaches inside another's implementation — branching into its code or altering its local data — which breaks the callee even when its interface is unchanged.

traps.title: Architecture is not the same as the design pattern list
traps.body: An architectural style constrains the whole system's component and connector types (pipe-and-filter, layered, repository). A design pattern solves a localised recurring problem (Observer, Factory). Questions mixing 'Singleton' into a list of architectural styles are testing this.

topics.title: Software Quality and Risk Management
topics.summary: McCall's eleven factors in three categories, ISO 9126, quality control versus assurance, risk identification and projection with numeric risk exposure, the RMMM plan, and reliability with MTTF, MTBF and availability.

blocks.text:
## What software quality means

The working definition used throughout the syllabus is Pressman's: software quality is **an effective software process applied in a manner that creates a useful product that provides measurable value for those who produce it and those who use it**. Three parts, each doing work. *Effective process* supplies the framework in which quality can be engineered rather than tested in afterwards. *Useful product* means the product delivers the content, functions and features the end user wants, reliably and error-free. *Adding value* means it makes the producer and the user better off — faster delivery for one, lower cost of ownership for the other.

Garvin's five views of quality are worth knowing because they explain why stakeholders disagree: the **transcendental** view (you recognise it when you see it), the **user** view (fitness for purpose), the **manufacturer** view (conformance to specification), the **product** view (inherent characteristics), and the **value-based** view (what a customer will pay).

Two definitions are routinely confused and routinely tested.

**Quality assurance (QA)** is *process*-oriented and *preventive*. It establishes and audits the processes, standards and procedures that will produce a quality product: process definition, audits, training, standards compliance, metrics collection.
