It asks "are we doing the right things, the right way?" and is the responsibility of the whole organisation.

**Quality control (QC)** is *product*-oriented and *corrective*. It is the series of inspections, reviews and tests applied to each work product to find defects: reviews, walkthroughs, inspections, testing. It asks "does this artefact meet its specification?"

A third term, **quality cost**, splits into **prevention costs** (planning, reviews training, tooling), **appraisal costs** (in-process inspection, equipment calibration, testing), and **failure costs** — **internal failure** (rework, repair, failure-mode analysis, found before shipping) and **external failure** (complaint resolution, product return, help-line support, warranty work, found after shipping). External failure cost is by far the largest, which is the economic argument for reviews.

## McCall's quality factors — eleven in three categories

McCall, Richards and Walters (1977) classified quality factors by what the software must do *over its life*. The three-way grouping and the membership of each group are asked directly.

### Product Operation — how well it runs now (5 factors)

| Factor | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| **Correctness** | Does it do what the specification says? |
| **Reliability** | Does it do it accurately every time, without failing? |
| **Efficiency** | How much computing resource and code does it need? |
| **Integrity** | Can unauthorised access to software and data be controlled? |
| **Usability** | What is the effort to learn, operate, prepare input and interpret output? |

### Product Revision — how well it can be changed (3 factors)

| Factor | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| **Maintainability** | What is the effort to locate and fix a fault? |
| **Flexibility** | What is the effort to modify an operational program? |
| **Testability** | What is the effort to test it and confirm it performs its function? |

### Product Transition — how well it can be moved (3 factors)

| Factor | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| **Portability** | What is the effort to move it to another hardware or software environment? |
| **Reusability** | Can it (or parts of it) be used in another application? |
| **Interoperability** | What is the effort to couple it to another system? |

Beneath the eleven factors McCall places a set of **quality criteria** (traceability, completeness, consistency, accuracy, error tolerance, execution efficiency, storage efficiency, access control, access audit, operability, training, communicativeness, simplicity, conciseness, instrumentation, self-documentation, expandability, generality, modularity, software system independence, machine independence, communications commonality, data commonality) which are given numeric grades 0 to 10 and combined with weights to score each factor.

**FURPS** (Hewlett-Packard) is a rival scheme: **Functionality, Usability, Reliability, Performance, Supportability**. **FURPS+** adds design, implementation, interface and physical constraints.

## ISO 9126 and ISO 25010

**ISO/IEC 9126** defines **six** quality characteristics, each with sub-characteristics. Remember the six as **F-R-U-E-M-P**.

| Characteristic | Sub-characteristics |
|---|---|
| **Functionality** | suitability, accuracy, interoperability, security, compliance |
| **Reliability** | maturity, fault tolerance, recoverability |
| **Usability** | understandability, learnability, operability, attractiveness |
| **Efficiency** | time behaviour, resource utilisation |
| **Maintainability** | analysability, changeability, stability, testability |
| **Portability** | adaptability, installability, co-existence, replaceability |

Two facts that separate 9126 from McCall in a question: **security is a sub-characteristic of Functionality in 9126**, whereas McCall gives it a top-level factor called Integrity; and **testability sits under Maintainability in 9126**, whereas McCall makes it a factor in its own right under Product Revision.

**ISO/IEC 25010**, the successor standard, raises the count to **eight** product quality characteristics by splitting out **Security** and **Compatibility** as top-level items: Functional suitability, Performance efficiency, Compatibility, Usability, Reliability, Security, Maintainability, Portability. If an option list has eight entries including Security, the standard being tested is 25010, not 9126.

## Software risk management

A **risk** is a potential problem: it has a **probability** of occurring and a **loss** (impact) if it does. Risk management is proactive when it identifies and plans for risks before they bite, and reactive — "firefighting", or the *Indiana Jones school* of risk management — when it responds only after the fact.

### Risk categories

By *what is threatened*:

- **Project risks** — threaten the plan: budget, schedule, staffing, resources, customer and requirements problems.
- **Technical risks** — threaten the quality and timeliness of the product: design, implementation, interface, verification and maintenance difficulties; leading-edge technology; ambiguous specification.
- **Business risks** — threaten the viability of the product. Five named sub-types: **market risk** (building something nobody wants), **strategic risk** (building something that no longer fits the business strategy), **sales risk** (building something the sales force does not know how to sell), **management risk** (losing the support of senior management), **budget risk** (losing budget or personnel commitment).

By *how well they can be foreseen*:

- **Known risks** — uncovered by careful evaluation of the plan, the environment and reliable information (unrealistic delivery date, no documented requirements, poor environment).
- **Predictable risks** — extrapolated from past project experience (staff turnover, poor customer communication).
- **Unpredictable risks** — can and do occur but are extremely hard to identify in advance.

### Risk identification and projection

Risk identification often uses a **risk item checklist** organised around product size, business impact, stakeholder characteristics, process definition, development environment, technology to be built, and staff size and experience. A *risk components and drivers* analysis assesses performance, cost, support and schedule risk, each rated for impact as **1 negligible, 2 marginal, 3 critical, 4 catastrophic** (note that on this scale the *lower* number is the *worse* outcome in some texts and the reverse in others — read the table given in the question).

**Risk projection (risk estimation)** has four activities: establish a scale reflecting the perceived likelihood of the risk; delineate the consequences; estimate the impact on the project and the product; and assess the overall accuracy of the projection so that misunderstandings do not follow.

### Risk exposure

The single computable quantity in the whole topic:

$$RE = P \times C$$

where $P$ is the probability the risk occurs and $C$ is the cost to the project if it does. $RE$ is in money, and it is the number used to rank the **risk table** and to justify how much may be spent on mitigation — spending more than $RE$ to avoid a risk is not rational.

The **risk table** lists each risk with its category, probability, impact and $RE$, sorted by probability and impact. A horizontal **cut-off line** is drawn; risks above it are actively managed, risks below it are re-evaluated periodically but not planned for.

blocks.title: Worked example — risk exposure and the risk table
blocks.text:
A project plans to build 60 reusable components. Three risks are identified.

**Risk R1.** Only 45 of the 60 components will actually be available for reuse; the remaining 15 must be built from scratch. Each component averages 120 LOC and costs \$16 per LOC. The probability of this risk is estimated at 60%.

$$C_1 = 15 \times 120 \times 16 = 15 \times 1920 = \$28{,}800$$
$$RE_1 = 0.60 \times 28{,}800 = \$17{,}280$$

**Risk R2.** A key database developer leaves during the project, costing 8 person-weeks of recovery at \$2,500 per person-week. Probability 25%.

$$C_2 = 8 \times 2500 = \$20{,}000, \qquad RE_2 = 0.25 \times 20{,}000 = \$5{,}000$$

**Risk R3.** The customer changes the reporting requirements late, forcing 200 LOC of rework at \$16 per LOC plus \$4,000 of re-testing. Probability 70%.

$$C_3 = 200 \times 16 + 4000 = 3200 + 4000 = \$7{,}200, \qquad RE_3 = 0.70 \times 7{,}200 = \$5{,}040$$

**Risk table, sorted by $RE$:**

| Risk | $P$ | $C$ | $RE$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 reuse shortfall | 0.60 | \$28,800 | **\$17,280** |
| R2 staff turnover | 0.25 | \$20,000 | \$5,000 |
| R3 requirements change | 0.70 | \$7,200 | \$5,040 |

**Total risk exposure** $= 17{,}280 + 5{,}000 + 5{,}040 = \$27{,}320$, which is the amount that should be carried as a risk reserve.

Two readings the examiner wants you to make. First, **R3 is the most likely risk but not the most serious one** — 70% probability with a small loss ranks third. Ranking by probability alone is the classic error; rank by $RE$. Second, it is worth spending up to \$17,280 to eliminate R1 entirely, and no more; a mitigation costing \$20,000 makes the project worse off.

## RMMM

The **RMMM plan** — **Risk Mitigation, Monitoring and Management** — documents all of the risk work. It can be a standalone document or a section of the software project plan; many teams instead keep a one-page **RIS (Risk Information Sheet)** per risk, holding the risk id, date, probability, impact, description, refinement, mitigation and monitoring approach, management/contingency plan and trigger, current status and the responsible person.

The three M's differ and are examined as a triple:

- **Mitigation** — act now to *reduce the probability or the impact*. For staff turnover: meet with staff to find causes, act on the controllable ones, organise teams so information is dispersed, define documentation standards, review work so that more than one person knows each module, assign a backup to every critical role.
- **Monitoring** — watch for indicators that tell you whether the risk is becoming more or less likely: team attitude, cohesion, relationships, availability of jobs elsewhere. Monitoring also checks whether the mitigation steps are being applied correctly.
- **Management** — assume the risk has occurred and execute the **contingency plan**: bring the backup person in, rely on the dispersed documentation, adjust the schedule.

A **risk trigger** is the observable event that says "switch from monitoring to management now". A useful rule of thumb is that RMMM costs should stay near 3–5% of total project cost.

Once a risk has been mitigated, the mitigation itself becomes a cost, so risk management adds project cost — and the judgement that must be made is whether the reduction in expected loss exceeds it.

## Software reliability

**Software reliability** is the probability of failure-free operation of a computer program in a specified environment for a specified time. Unlike hardware, software does not wear out, so its failures come from latent design faults, not from physical degradation — which is why the software failure-rate curve is an *idealised* falling curve, and the *actual* curve rises in steps each time a change introduces new faults before falling again.

The measurable quantities:

| Symbol | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **MTTF** | mean time to failure | average operating time before a failure occurs |
| **MTTR** | mean time to repair | average time to diagnose and correct a failure |
| **MTBF** | mean time between failures | $\text{MTTF} + \text{MTTR}$ |

$$\text{MTBF} = \text{MTTF} + \text{MTTR}$$

$$\text{Availability} = \frac{\text{MTTF}}{\text{MTTF} + \text{MTTR}} \times 100\% = \frac{\text{MTTF}}{\text{MTBF}} \times 100\%$$

For a constant failure rate $\lambda$ (the exponential failure model):

$$\lambda = \frac{1}{\text{MTTF}}, \qquad R(t) = e^{-\lambda t} = e^{-t/\text{MTTF}}$$

Other reliability metrics used in the syllabus: **POFOD** (probability of failure on demand — the right metric for a protection system that is idle most of the time), **ROCOF** (rate of occurrence of failures — the right metric for a transaction system), **AVAIL** (availability, for a continuously running system).

**Software safety** is a related but distinct discipline: it identifies **hazards** (conditions that can cause an accident) and analyses them with fault tree analysis, real-time logic or petri nets. A system can be reliable and unsafe — it can execute its specification perfectly and still cause harm because the specification was wrong.

blocks.title: Worked example — MTTF, MTBF, availability and reliability
blocks.text:
A transaction server runs for 1,000 hours and records 5 failures. The total downtime for repairs across those failures was 20 hours.

**Uptime** $= 1000 - 20 = 980$ hours.

$$\text{MTTF} = \frac{\text{total uptime}}{\text{number of failures}} = \frac{980}{5} = 196 \text{ hours}$$
$$\text{MTTR} = \frac{\text{total downtime}}{\text{number of failures}} = \frac{20}{5} = 4 \text{ hours}$$
$$\text{MTBF} = 196 + 4 = 200 \text{ hours}$$
$$\text{Availability} = \frac{196}{200} \times 100\% = 98\%$$

Sanity check from the other direction: total time $1000 = 5 \times \text{MTBF} = 5 \times 200$. Consistent.

**Failure rate.** $\lambda = 1/196 \approx 0.0051$ failures per hour, i.e. about 5.1 failures per 1000 operating hours.

**Reliability over a 24-hour mission.**
$$R(24) = e^{-24/196} = e^{-0.1224} = 0.8848$$
so there is an 88.5% chance of running a full day without a failure.

**A second version.** Suppose instead MTTF = 900 hours and MTTR = 100 hours.
$$\text{MTBF} = 1000 \text{ h}, \qquad \text{Availability} = \frac{900}{1000} = 90\%$$
Notice that availability fell from 98% to 90% even though the *reliability* per hour of operation is far better in the second system ($\lambda = 1/900$ against $1/196$). Availability rewards fast repair; reliability rewards not failing. A question that gives MTTF and MTTR and asks for "reliability" almost always wants availability — read which one it defines.

blocks.title: MTBF is not MTTF
blocks.text:
$\text{MTBF} = \text{MTTF} + \text{MTTR}$. MTTF measures only the *running* interval; MTBF measures the full cycle from one failure to the next, including the repair.

Availability uses **MTTF in the numerator and MTBF in the denominator** — never MTBF over MTTF, which would exceed 1, and never MTTR anywhere in the numerator.

When a question gives 'operating time' and 'number of failures' with no downtime mentioned, MTTF and MTBF coincide and availability is 100%; that is the degenerate case, not an error.

blocks.q: Maintainability, Flexibility and Testability are the three McCall quality factors in the category
blocks.exp: Product Operation holds five factors (correctness, reliability, efficiency, integrity, usability); Product Revision holds the three that concern changing the software (maintainability, flexibility, testability); Product Transition holds the three that concern moving it (portability, reusability, interoperability). There is no category called Product Conformance.

blocks.q: A risk has a 40% probability of occurring and would cost the project $75,000. Which mitigation decision is economically justified?
opts: Spend up to $75,000 to eliminate it
Spend up to $30,000 to eliminate it
Spend nothing, because the probability is below 50%
Spend $40,000 because that matches the probability
blocks.exp: Risk exposure is $RE = P \times C = 0.40 \times 75{,}000 = \$30{,}000$, the expected loss. Spending more than the expected loss to remove the risk leaves the project worse off, so $30,000 is the ceiling. Probability alone never decides the question — a 40% risk of a large loss can outrank a 90% risk of a trivial one.

blocks.q: A system has MTTF = 450 hours and MTTR = 50 hours. Its availability is
blocks.exp: MTBF = MTTF + MTTR = 450 + 50 = 500 hours, and availability = MTTF/MTBF = 450/500 = 0.90, i.e. 90%. The distractor 88.9% comes from dividing by MTTF+2·MTTR or from using 400/450; 11.1% is the complement of 88.9% and corresponds to computing MTTR/MTTF.

tricks.title: McCall 5-3-3
tricks.body: Operation has five factors, Revision three, Transition three — eleven in total. If you can recall only the counts, the three-item groups are the changeability group (maintainability, flexibility, testability) and the movability group (portability, reusability, interoperability); everything else is Operation.

tricks.title: 9126 has six, 25010 has eight
tricks.body: Count the options. Six characteristics with security buried under Functionality means ISO 9126. Eight characteristics with Security and Compatibility standing alone means ISO 25010. Any list containing 'Correctness' or 'Integrity' is McCall, not ISO.

tricks.title: Rank risks by RE, never by probability
tricks.body: Every risk-table question includes one high-probability, low-cost risk as a decoy for first place. Compute $P \times C$ for every row before answering, and remember the answer to 'how much may we spend' is exactly $RE$.

tricks.title: Availability = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR)
tricks.body: Write MTBF underneath before dividing. From raw data, MTTF = total uptime / failures and MTTR = total downtime / failures, so the number of failures cancels and availability is simply uptime / total time.

tricks.title: QA prevents, QC detects
tricks.body: Any activity that defines, audits or trains on a process is assurance; any activity that inspects a specific artefact — review, walkthrough, inspection, test — is control. A single keyword in the option usually settles it.

traps.title: Reliability and safety are not the same thing
traps.body: Reliability is conformance to the specification over time; safety is freedom from hazardous behaviour. A program can be perfectly reliable and still unsafe if the specification itself allows a dangerous state. Options equating the two are wrong.

traps.title: Software does not wear out — but its failure rate is not flat
traps.body: The idealised curve falls and then stays flat; the actual curve steps upward at each change because maintenance introduces new faults, then decays again. 'Software failure rate stays constant after release' is false in the realistic model.

traps.title: Risk exposure is money, not a probability
traps.body: $RE$ has the units of the cost $C$. A question offering an $RE$ between 0 and 1 is offering the probability back to you as a distractor.

traps.title: Testability appears in both schemes, at different levels
traps.body: McCall makes testability a top-level factor under Product Revision; ISO 9126 makes it a sub-characteristic of Maintainability. Similarly, McCall's Integrity corresponds to 9126's Security sub-characteristic of Functionality. Answer according to the scheme the question names.

topics.title: Estimation and Scheduling: LOC, FP, COCOMO
topics.summary: Sizing with LOC and a fully worked function point count, the three COCOMO modes with exact coefficients, COCOMO II, the Putnam software equation, and scheduling with the 40-20-40 rule.

blocks.text:
## The estimation chain

Every estimate in software engineering follows the same three links: **size → effort → schedule and cost**. You cannot estimate effort without first estimating size, and you cannot lay out a schedule without first estimating effort. Every model in this topic sits at one of those links.

| Link | Techniques |
|---|---|
| Size | LOC, function points, object points, Halstead's length |
| Effort | COCOMO (basic, intermediate, detailed), COCOMO II, Putnam/SLIM, empirical productivity, expert judgement, Delphi |
| Schedule | COCOMO duration equation, Putnam's time-effort trade-off, timeline chart / Gantt, PERT and CPM |

Estimation options in decreasing order of reliability are: delay the estimate until late in the project (accurate but useless), base it on similar completed projects, decompose the problem, or use an empirical model. In practice you decompose *and* apply a model, and cross-check one against the other.

**Three-point (PERT-style) size estimation** smooths the guesswork. With an optimistic size $a$, a most likely size $m$ and a pessimistic size $b$, the expected value is

$$EV = \frac{a + 4m + b}{6}$$

For example, with $a = 4600$, $m = 6900$ and $b = 8600$ LOC, $EV = (4600 + 27600 + 8600)/6 = 40800/6 = \mathbf{6800}$ LOC.

## LOC as a size measure

Lines of code is the oldest and simplest size metric: count delivered source statements, usually excluding comments and blank lines, and quote it in **KLOC** (thousands of lines). From it come the standard productivity and quality metrics:

$$\text{Productivity} = \frac{\text{KLOC}}{\text{person-months}}, \qquad \text{Cost per LOC} = \frac{\text{total cost}}{\text{LOC}}, \qquad \text{Defect density} = \frac{\text{defects}}{\text{KLOC}}$$

LOC has two structural defects. It is **language dependent** — the same functionality takes about four times as many lines in C as in a fourth-generation language, so a productive team using a better language scores worse. And it is **not available until the code is written**, which makes it useless at the time an estimate is actually needed, unless historical LOC-per-function figures are used.

**Halstead's software science** derives size and effort from operator and operand counts. With $n_1$ distinct operators, $n_2$ distinct operands, $N_1$ total operator occurrences and $N_2$ total operand occurrences:

$$n = n_1 + n_2 \ \text{(vocabulary)}, \qquad N = N_1 + N_2 \ \text{(length)}$$
$$\hat{N} = n_1 \log_2 n_1 + n_2 \log_2 n_2 \ \text{(estimated length)}, \qquad V = N \log_2 n \ \text{(volume)}$$
$$D = \frac{n_1}{2} \cdot \frac{N_2}{n_2} \ \text{(difficulty)}, \qquad E = D \times V \ \text{(effort)}, \qquad T = \frac{E}{18} \ \text{seconds}$$

For the fragment `a = b + c; d = a * b;` the distinct operators are `=`, `+`, `*`, `;` so $n_1 = 4$ with $N_1 = 2+1+1+2 = 6$; the distinct operands are `a`, `b`, `c`, `d` so $n_2 = 4$ with $N_2 = 2+2+1+1 = 6$. Then $n = 8$, $N = 12$, $V = 12\log_2 8 = 36$, $D = (4/2)(6/4) = 3$, $E = 108$ and $T = 6$ seconds.

## Function points

Albrecht's function point metric measures size in terms of **functionality delivered to the user**, which makes it language independent and — crucially — computable from the requirements, before any code exists.

### The five information domain values

| Value | What it counts |
|---|---|
| **External Inputs (EI)** | distinct user or control data items that enter and alter internal data |
| **External Outputs (EO)** | derived data leaving the system — reports, screens, error messages (a report is one EO, not one per data item) |
| **External Inquiries (EQ)** | an online input that causes an immediate response with no derivation and no update of internal files |
| **Internal Logical Files (ILF)** | logical groupings of data maintained *inside* the application boundary |
| **External Interface Files (EIF)** | logical groupings of data read from, but maintained by, another application |

### The weighting table

Each count is placed in one of three complexity bands:

| Information domain value | Simple | Average | Complex |
|---|---|---|---|
| External Inputs (EI) | 3 | 4 | 6 |
| External Outputs (EO) | 4 | 5 | 7 |
| External Inquiries (EQ) | 3 | 4 | 6 |
| Internal Logical Files (ILF) | 7 | 10 | 15 |
| External Interface Files (EIF) | 5 | 7 | 10 |

The weighted sum is the **Unadjusted Function Point count, UFP** (also called the count total).

### The fourteen general system characteristics

Each of the fourteen is rated **0 (no influence) to 5 (essential)**, so $\sum F_i$ ranges from 0 to 70.

1. Data communications
2. Distributed data processing
3. Performance requirements
4. Heavily used configuration
5. Transaction rate
6. Online data entry
7. End-user efficiency
8. Online update
9. Complex processing
10. Reusability
11. Installation ease
12. Operational ease
13. Multiple sites / organisations
14. Facilitate change

### The final formula

$$\text{VAF} = 0.65 + 0.01 \sum_{i=1}^{14} F_i, \qquad \boxed{\text{FP} = \text{UFP} \times \left(0.65 + 0.01 \sum F_i\right)}$$

Because $\sum F_i \in [0, 70]$, the value adjustment factor lies in $[0.65, 1.35]$: the adjustment can move the count by at most **±35%**. Those three numbers — 0.65, 0.01, 14 — are the ones examiners check.

Function points convert into LOC through published **backfiring** factors: roughly 320 LOC/FP in assembly, 128 in C, 105 in COBOL, 53 in Java, 29 in C++, 15 in SQL. Productivity and quality can then be quoted per function point: FP per person-month, cost per FP, defects per FP, pages of documentation per FP.

**Feature points** and **3D function points** extend the idea to algorithmically intensive and real-time software by adding an algorithm count and control-dimension counts. **Object points** (used by COCOMO II's application composition model) count screens, reports and 3GL components, weighted simple/medium/difficult.

blocks.title: Worked example — a complete function point count
blocks.text:
A claims-processing application is analysed and the following counts are obtained.

| Domain value | Simple | Average | Complex |
|---|---|---|---|
| External Inputs | 8 | 6 | 2 |
| External Outputs | 0 | 5 | 3 |
| External Inquiries | 10 | 2 | 0 |
| Internal Logical Files | 0 | 3 | 1 |
| External Interface Files | 2 | 0 | 0 |

**Step 1 — apply the weights row by row.**

$$\text{EI} = 8(3) + 6(4) + 2(6) = 24 + 24 + 12 = 60$$
$$\text{EO} = 0(4) + 5(5) + 3(7) = 0 + 25 + 21 = 46$$
$$\text{EQ} = 10(3) + 2(4) + 0(6) = 30 + 8 + 0 = 38$$
$$\text{ILF} = 0(7) + 3(10) + 1(15) = 0 + 30 + 15 = 45$$
$$\text{EIF} = 2(5) + 0(7) + 0(10) = 10$$

**Step 2 — unadjusted function points.**

$$\text{UFP} = 60 + 46 + 38 + 45 + 10 = \mathbf{199}$$

**Step 3 — the fourteen characteristics.** Suppose the ratings are

| # | Characteristic | $F_i$ | # | Characteristic | $F_i$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Data communications | 4 | 8 | Online update | 4 |
| 2 | Distributed processing | 2 | 9 | Complex processing | 3 |
| 3 | Performance | 4 | 10 | Reusability | 2 |
| 4 | Heavily used configuration | 3 | 11 | Installation ease | 3 |
| 5 | Transaction rate | 5 | 12 | Operational ease | 4 |
| 6 | Online data entry | 5 | 13 | Multiple sites | 2 |
| 7 | End-user efficiency | 4 | 14 | Facilitate change | 1 |

$$\sum F_i = 4+2+4+3+5+5+4+4+3+2+3+4+2+1$$

Add in pairs: $(4+2)=6$, $(4+3)=7 \Rightarrow 13$, $(5+5)=10 \Rightarrow 23$, $(4+4)=8 \Rightarrow 31$, $(3+2)=5 \Rightarrow 36$, $(3+4)=7 \Rightarrow 43$, $(2+1)=3 \Rightarrow \mathbf{46}$.

**Step 4 — value adjustment factor and final count.**

$$\text{VAF} = 0.65 + 0.01(46) = 0.65 + 0.46 = 1.11$$
$$\text{FP} = 199 \times 1.11 = \mathbf{220.89} \approx 221$$

**Step 5 — use the number.** If the organisation's historical productivity on similar work is 6.5 FP per person-month and the loaded labour rate is \$4,000 per person-month:

$$\text{Effort} = \frac{220.89}{6.5} = 33.98 \approx 34 \text{ person-months}, \qquad \text{Cost} = 34 \times 4000 = \$136{,}000$$
$$\text{Cost per FP} = \frac{136{,}000}{220.89} = \$615.7$$

**Step 6 — convert to LOC if a LOC-driven model is wanted.** In Java at 53 LOC/FP:

$$\text{LOC} = 220.89 \times 53 = 11{,}707 \approx \mathbf{11.7\ KLOC}$$

which is the size that would then be fed to COCOMO.

## COCOMO — the Constructive Cost Model

Boehm's 1981 model estimates effort in **person-months (PM)** and development time in **months** from size in **KLOC**. Three *modes* describe the project, and three *levels* describe how much detail the model uses.

### The three modes

| Mode | Team and problem | Typical size |
|---|---|---|
| **Organic** | small team, familiar application, flexible requirements, in-house | under about 50 KLOC |
| **Semi-detached** | mixed experience, mix of rigid and flexible requirements | 50–300 KLOC |
| **Embedded** | tight hardware, software and operational constraints; a change is very expensive | over about 300 KLOC |

The size boundaries are indicative only; the mode is really determined by constraint and familiarity, not by size, and a question that describes "real-time software embedded in hardware with tight coupling" means the embedded mode regardless of the KLOC given.

### Basic COCOMO

$$E = a\,(\text{KLOC})^{b} \ \text{person-months}, \qquad D = c\,(E)^{d} \ \text{months}, \qquad N = \frac{E}{D} \ \text{persons}$$

| Mode | $a$ | $b$ | $c$ | $d$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Organic** | **2.4** | **1.05** | **2.5** | **0.38** |
| **Semi-detached** | **3.0** | **1.12** | **2.5** | **0.35** |
| **Embedded** | **3.6** | **1.20** | **2.5** | **0.32** |

Every exponent $b$ exceeds 1, so effort grows **superlinearly** with size — doubling the code more than doubles the effort. Every $c$ is 2.5 and every $d$ is less than 1, so schedule grows **sublinearly** with effort, which is why huge projects take only moderately longer but cost enormously more. Memorise the column $c = 2.5$ for all three modes; it is free marks.

### Intermediate COCOMO

Adds an **Effort Adjustment Factor (EAF)**, the product of 15 cost drivers each rated very low to extra high:

$$E = a\,(\text{KLOC})^{b} \times \text{EAF}$$

| Mode | $a$ | $b$ |
|---|---|---|
| **Organic** | **3.2** | 1.05 |
| **Semi-detached** | **3.0** | 1.12 |
| **Embedded** | **2.8** | 1.20 |

Note the pattern flip: the exponents are unchanged but the multipliers now *decrease* from organic to embedded, because the harshness of an embedded project is carried by the cost drivers instead. A nominal project has EAF = 1.0; a typical EAF range is about 0.9 to 1.4.

The 15 cost drivers fall into four groups: **product attributes** (RELY required reliability, DATA database size, CPLX product complexity), **hardware/computer attributes** (TIME execution time constraint, STOR main storage constraint, VIRT virtual machine volatility, TURN turnaround time), **personnel attributes** (ACAP analyst capability, AEXP applications experience, PCAP programmer capability, VEXP virtual machine experience, LEXP language experience), and **project attributes** (MODP modern programming practices, TOOL use of software tools, SCED required development schedule).

**Detailed (complete) COCOMO** applies the cost drivers **phase by phase** — requirements, design, coding, integration and test — rather than to the whole project, and adds a three-level hierarchy of module, subsystem and system.

blocks.title: Worked example — COCOMO for all three modes at 32 KLOC
blocks.text:
A system is estimated at **32 KLOC**. Compute basic COCOMO effort, duration and average staffing for each mode. (All logarithms base $e$; results rounded to two decimals.)

### Organic: $a=2.4,\ b=1.05,\ c=2.5,\ d=0.38$

$$E = 2.4 \times 32^{1.05}$$
$\ln 32 = 3.4657$, so $32^{1.05} = e^{1.05 \times 3.4657} = e^{3.6390} = 38.05$.
$$E = 2.4 \times 38.05 = \mathbf{91.33 \text{ PM}}$$
$$D = 2.5 \times 91.33^{0.38}$$
$\ln 91.33 = 4.5146$, so $91.33^{0.38} = e^{1.7155} = 5.559$.
$$D = 2.5 \times 5.559 = \mathbf{13.90 \text{ months}}$$
$$N = \frac{91.33}{13.90} = 6.57 \approx \mathbf{7 \text{ people}}$$

### Semi-detached: $a=3.0,\ b=1.12,\ c=2.5,\ d=0.35$

$32^{1.12} = e^{1.12 \times 3.4657} = e^{3.8816} = 48.50$.
$$E = 3.0 \times 48.50 = \mathbf{145.51 \text{ PM}}$$
$\ln 145.51 = 4.9802$, so $145.51^{0.35} = e^{1.7431} = 5.714$.
$$D = 2.5 \times 5.714 = \mathbf{14.29 \text{ months}}, \qquad N = \frac{145.51}{14.29} = 10.18 \approx \mathbf{11 \text{ people}}$$

### Embedded: $a=3.6,\ b=1.20,\ c=2.5,\ d=0.32$

Here the arithmetic is exact: $32 = 2^5$, so $32^{1.2} = 2^{6} = 64$.
$$E = 3.6 \times 64 = \mathbf{230.4 \text{ PM}}$$
$\ln 230.4 = 5.4399$, so $230.4^{0.32} = e^{1.7408} = 5.701$.
$$D = 2.5 \times 5.701 = \mathbf{14.25 \text{ months}}, \qquad N = \frac{230.4}{14.25} = 16.17 \approx \mathbf{17 \text{ people}}$$

### Reading the table

| Mode | Effort (PM) | Duration (mo) | Staff |
|---|---|---|---|
| Organic | 91.33 | 13.90 | 7 |
| Semi-detached | 145.51 | 14.29 | 11 |
| Embedded | 230.40 | 14.25 | 17 |

The effort ratio embedded : organic is $230.4/91.33 = 2.52$ — two and a half times the cost for the same 32 KLOC — while the durations differ by less than half a month. The mode changes **how many people you need**, not **how long it takes**. That is the single most useful observation in the topic.

### Adding an EAF (intermediate COCOMO)

Suppose the same 32 KLOC is organic but has high reliability requirements (RELY = 1.15), an experienced team (ACAP = 0.86) and heavy use of tools (TOOL = 0.91). Then

$$\text{EAF} = 1.15 \times 0.86 \times 0.91 = 0.900$$
$$E = 3.2 \times 32^{1.05} \times 0.900 = 3.2 \times 38.05 \times 0.900 = 121.76 \times 0.900 = \mathbf{109.58 \text{ PM}}$$

using the intermediate organic coefficient $a = 3.2$, not the basic $2.4$. Mixing those two coefficients is the most common arithmetic error in this topic.

## COCOMO II

The 1990s revision replaces the single model with **three** models used at different points in the life cycle:

| Model | When used | Size measured in |
|---|---|---|
| **Application composition** | early prototyping, integration-intensive work | **object points** |
| **Early design** | after requirements are stable, before architecture | **function points** converted to KSLOC; **7** effort multipliers |
| **Post-architecture** | after the architecture is defined | KSLOC or FP; **17** effort multipliers and **5** scale factors |

The application composition model computes new object points as $\text{NOP} = \text{object points} \times (1 - \% \text{reuse}/100)$ and divides by a productivity rate (4 for very low developer experience and maturity, 7 low, 13 nominal, 25 high, 50 very high NOP per person-month).

The post-architecture effort equation is

$$\text{PM} = A \times (\text{Size})^{E} \times \prod_{i=1}^{17} \text{EM}_i, \qquad E = B + 0.01 \sum_{j=1}^{5} SF_j$$

with $A = 2.94$ and $B = 0.91$. The five **scale factors** are **PREC** (precedentedness), **FLEX** (development flexibility), **RESL** (architecture and risk resolution), **TEAM** (team cohesion) and **PMAT** (process maturity); each is rated very low to extra high, contributing between 0 and about 6.2 points. So $E$ ranges roughly from 0.91 to 1.23 — the exponent is *estimated*, not fixed by a mode, which is COCOMO II's main conceptual advance over COCOMO 81.

For example, with $\sum SF = 15$, $E = 0.91 + 0.15 = 1.06$; at 100 KSLOC and nominal multipliers, $\text{PM} = 2.94 \times 100^{1.06} = 2.94 \times 131.83 = 387.6$ person-months.

## The Putnam model (SLIM) and the software equation

Putnam's model comes from fitting a **Rayleigh curve** to the manpower build-up observed on large projects. The **software equation** in its classic form is

$$L = C_k \, K^{1/3} \, t_d^{4/3}$$

where $L$ is size in LOC, $C_k$ is a **technology constant** (about 2,000 for a poor environment, 8,000 for a good one, 11,000 for an excellent one), $K$ is the **total life-cycle effort in person-years**, and $t_d$ is the **development time in years**. Rearranged for effort:

$$K = \frac{L^3}{C_k^{3} \, t_d^{4}}$$

The exponent 4 on $t_d$ is the whole point and is known as the **fourth power trade-off law**: effort varies inversely with the *fourth power* of the development time. Shortening the schedule by a modest amount multiplies the effort enormously, which is Putnam's quantitative version of Brooks's observation that adding people to a late project makes it later.

Pressman's equivalent statement uses a productivity parameter $P$ and a special skills factor $B$:

$$E = \left[\frac{\text{LOC} \times B^{0.333}}{P}\right]^{3} \times \frac{1}{t^{4}}$$

and the minimum development time is $t_{\min} = 8.14 (\text{LOC}/P)^{0.43}$ months for $t_{\min} > 6$ months.

COCOMO carries the same warning in a different form: the schedule should not be compressed below about **75% of the nominal** duration, because below that the required effort rises faster than the saving in time.

blocks.title: Worked example — the fourth power trade-off
blocks.text:
A project is sized at **50,000 LOC** in an environment with technology constant $C_k = 10{,}000$.

**At $t_d = 2$ years:**

$$K = \frac{L^3}{C_k^3 t_d^4} = \frac{(5 \times 10^4)^3}{(10^4)^3 \times 2^4} = \frac{1.25 \times 10^{14}}{10^{12} \times 16} = \frac{1.25 \times 10^{14}}{1.6 \times 10^{13}} = \mathbf{7.81 \text{ person-years}}$$

**Management now asks for delivery in 1.5 years.**

$$K = \frac{1.25 \times 10^{14}}{10^{12} \times (1.5)^4} = \frac{1.25 \times 10^{14}}{10^{12} \times 5.0625} = \frac{1.25 \times 10^{14}}{5.0625 \times 10^{12}} = \mathbf{24.69 \text{ person-years}}$$

**The ratio.** Cutting the schedule by 25% multiplied the effort by

$$\frac{24.69}{7.81} = 3.16 = \left(\frac{2}{1.5}\right)^4 = \left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^4 = \frac{256}{81} = 3.16$$

Three times the cost for one quarter less time. Notice the shortcut: you never need the absolute numbers to answer a ratio question — the effort ratio is simply the inverse fourth power of the time ratio.

**Going the other way.** If the schedule were relaxed to 2.5 years,
$$K = \frac{1.25 \times 10^{14}}{10^{12} \times 39.0625} = 3.2 \text{ person-years},$$
a 59% saving for 6 extra months. That asymmetry is why Putnam's model is used to argue *against* compression rather than to plan it.

## Scheduling

Once effort is known it must be distributed over time and over people. The principles are:

- **Compartmentalisation** — divide the product and process into a manageable number of activities and tasks.
- **Interdependency** — determine which tasks must be sequential and which may run in parallel.
- **Time allocation** — give every task a start date, an end date and a number of work units.
- **Effort validation** — never allocate more people at any point than are available.
- **Defined responsibilities, defined outcomes, defined milestones** — every task has an owner, a work product and a reviewable end point.

### The 40-20-40 rule

The classic distribution of effort across the life cycle is **40% front end (analysis and design), 20% coding, 40% testing and debugging**. In more detail: 2–3% planning, 10–25% requirements analysis, 20–25% design, 15–20% coding, 30–40% testing and debugging. The rule's real message is that **coding is the smallest of the three phases** and that testing consumes as much as analysis and design together — the opposite of the naive assumption. Only the 40-20-40 split needs memorising; the percentages within the front end vary by source.

### Tools

A **work breakdown structure (WBS)** decomposes the project into tasks. A **task network (activity network)** shows their dependencies and yields the **critical path** — the longest chain of dependent tasks, which fixes the minimum project duration and has zero slack. A **timeline chart** or **Gantt chart** plots each task as a horizontal bar against a calendar, with **milestones** as diamonds; it shows what runs in parallel and where the slack is. **PERT** and **CPM** add the quantitative machinery: earliest and latest start and finish times, total float, and the probabilistic three-point duration estimate.

Progress is tracked by **earned value analysis**: with BCWS (budgeted cost of work scheduled), BCWP (budgeted cost of work performed) and ACWP (actual cost of work performed),

$$\text{SPI} = \frac{\text{BCWP}}{\text{BCWS}}, \qquad \text{CPI} = \frac{\text{BCWP}}{\text{ACWP}}, \qquad \text{SV} = \text{BCWP} - \text{BCWS}, \qquad \text{CV} = \text{BCWP} - \text{ACWP}$$

An index above 1 is good; below 1 means behind schedule (SPI) or over budget (CPI).

blocks.title: Worked example — distributing effort and reading a schedule
blocks.text:
Take the organic 32 KLOC estimate from above: $E = 91.33$ PM over $D = 13.90$ months with an average of 7 people.

**Apply 40-20-40.**

$$\text{Analysis and design} = 0.40 \times 91.33 = 36.53 \text{ PM}$$
$$\text{Coding} = 0.20 \times 91.33 = 18.27 \text{ PM}$$
$$\text{Testing and debugging} = 0.40 \times 91.33 = 36.53 \text{ PM}$$

Check: $36.53 + 18.27 + 36.53 = 91.33$. ✓

**Convert to calendar time at constant staffing of 7 people.** Analysis and design: $36.53/7 = 5.22$ months. Coding: $18.27/7 = 2.61$ months. Testing: $5.22$ months. Total $13.05$ months, slightly under the 13.90 the model predicts — the difference is the staffing ramp-up and ramp-down that a constant headcount ignores.

**A schedule-compression question.** Management wants delivery in 10 months instead of 13.90. That is $10/13.90 = 72\%$ of nominal, below COCOMO's 75% floor, so the answer expected is that the compression is **not feasible**; the achievable minimum is $0.75 \times 13.90 = 10.4$ months, and even that costs extra effort.

**Earned value at month 7.** Suppose BCWS = 45 PM, BCWP = 40 PM and ACWP = 48 PM.

$$\text{SPI} = 40/45 = 0.89 \ (\text{behind schedule}), \qquad \text{CPI} = 40/48 = 0.83 \ (\text{over budget})$$
$$\text{SV} = 40 - 45 = -5 \text{ PM}, \qquad \text{CV} = 40 - 48 = -8 \text{ PM}$$

Both indices below 1 and both variances negative: the project has done less work than planned and spent more than it should have for the work it did.

| | $a$ | $b$ | $d$ | (intermediate $a$) |

| Organic | 2.4 | 1.05 | 0.38 | 3.2 |

**Three-point** $EV = (a + 4m + b)/6$. **Effort split** 40-20-40.

blocks.q: An application has UFP = 300 and all fourteen general system characteristics rated 3. Its adjusted function point count is
blocks.exp: $\sum F_i = 14 \times 3 = 42$, so VAF $= 0.65 + 0.01 \times 42 = 1.07$ and FP $= 300 \times 1.07 = 321$. The distractor 324 comes from using 0.68 as the base constant, and 348 from adding 0.01 times 48. Always compute $\sum F_i$ first and check it lies between 0 and 70.

blocks.q: For a 32 KLOC embedded-mode project, basic COCOMO gives an effort of
blocks.exp: Embedded uses $a = 3.6$ and $b = 1.20$, so $E = 3.6 \times 32^{1.2}$. Since $32 = 2^5$, $32^{1.2} = 2^6 = 64$ exactly, giving $E = 3.6 \times 64 = 230.4$ PM. The other options are the organic (2.4, 1.05) and semi-detached (3.0, 1.12) results for the same size.

blocks.q: Using Putnam's software equation, if the development time is reduced from 3 years to 2 years with size and technology constant unchanged, the required effort is multiplied by approximately
blocks.exp: Effort varies as $1/t_d^4$, so the multiplier is $(3/2)^4 = 81/16 = 5.0625$. The distractors are the ratio itself (1.5), its square (2.25) and its cube (3.375) — the exponent on time in $K = L^3/(C_k^3 t_d^4)$ is 4, not 1, 2 or 3.

tricks.title: Pick powers of two for COCOMO arithmetic
tricks.body: When KLOC is a power of two the embedded exponent 1.20 often lands exactly: $32^{1.2} = 2^{6} = 64$, $64^{1.2} = 2^{7.2}$, $16^{1.2}=2^{4.8}$. Check for that before reaching for logarithms; exam setters choose sizes that make one mode come out clean.

tricks.title: c = 2.5 in every mode
tricks.body: The duration coefficient is 2.5 for organic, semi-detached and embedded alike. Only the exponent $d$ changes: 0.38, 0.35, 0.32 — decreasing as the mode gets harder, which is why durations barely differ between modes while efforts differ by a factor of two and a half.

tricks.title: Putnam ratios need no absolute numbers
tricks.body: For 'by what factor does effort change if the schedule changes', use $K_1/K_2 = (t_2/t_1)^4$ directly. Size and $C_k$ cancel, so you never compute $L^3$.

tricks.title: VAF is bounded, so sanity-check the answer
tricks.body: FP can be at most $1.35 \times$ UFP and at least $0.65 \times$ UFP. If your adjusted count is more than 35% away from the unadjusted one, you have mis-added $\sum F_i$ or used the wrong constants.

tricks.title: Basic a versus intermediate a
tricks.body: Basic COCOMO multipliers go up with difficulty (2.4, 3.0, 3.6); intermediate multipliers go down (3.2, 3.0, 2.8). Semi-detached is 3.0 in both, which is the anchor. If the question mentions an EAF or cost drivers, it is intermediate; if it gives only size and mode, it is basic.

traps.title: Do not multiply UFP by the wrong constant
traps.body: The formula is $0.65 + 0.01\sum F_i$, not $0.65 + 0.001\sum F_i$ and not $0.65 \times \sum F_i$. With all fourteen factors at their maximum of 5, $\sum F_i = 70$ and VAF $= 1.35$; with all at 0, VAF $= 0.65$. Any answer outside that band is arithmetically impossible.

traps.title: An external output is one report, not one field
traps.body: Counting information domain values is where marks are lost. One screen or report is one EO regardless of how many data items it shows; one logical file is one ILF regardless of how many physical tables implement it; and an EQ is an input-plus-response pair with no derivation and no file update, so a query that also writes an audit record is an EI, not an EQ.

traps.title: COCOMO's D uses effort, not size
traps.body: $D = 2.5 E^{d}$ takes the effort you just computed as its argument. Substituting KLOC into the duration equation is a standard error and produces a duration that is far too small for large projects.

traps.title: 40-20-40 is not 40% coding
traps.body: The middle number is coding and it is the smallest: 40% analysis and design, 20% coding, 40% testing and debugging. An option reading '40-40-20' with testing last is the distractor.

traps.title: Person-months are not interchangeable with months
traps.body: Effort $E$ and duration $D$ are different quantities and $N = E/D$ is the average team size, not the total. Doubling the team does not halve the duration — COCOMO's own floor of 75% of nominal duration says so explicitly.
