blocks.text:
## Verification, validation, and what testing can prove

Two questions look alike and are not.

**Verification** — *are we building the product right?* It checks each work product against its specification. It is largely **static**: reviews, walkthroughs, inspections, desk checks, static analysis. It happens continuously, from the SRS onwards.

**Validation** — *are we building the right product?* It checks the finished system against the customer's actual needs. It is largely **dynamic**: you run the software. Acceptance testing is the canonical validation activity.

Verification catches an SRS requirement implemented incorrectly. Validation catches a requirement that was implemented perfectly and was the wrong requirement. A system can pass every verification step and still fail validation.

The other vocabulary distinction, from IEEE 610.12 and ISO 24765:

| Term | Where it lives | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| **Error** (mistake) | in a person's head | a human action that produces an incorrect result |
| **Fault / Defect / Bug** | in the artefact | the incorrect step, process or data definition that the error produced |
| **Failure** | in the behaviour | the inability of the system to perform a required function — an observed deviation from expected behaviour |

The causal chain is **error → fault → failure**. A fault that is never executed, or is executed without propagating to output, produces no failure — which is why testing can show the presence of faults but never their absence (Dijkstra). *Error* is also used loosely for the difference between a computed and a correct value; in the exam, if the options include all three terms, use the chain above.

Testing objectives, stated in Glen Myers's classic form: testing is a process of executing a program with the **intent of finding an error**; a good test case has a high probability of finding an as-yet-undiscovered error; a successful test is one that **uncovers** an undiscovered error. So a test that passes has, in this vocabulary, failed in its objective — a favourite true/false item.

## Testability and the strategy

Software testability is how easily a program can be tested. Bach's attributes: **operability** (it works well enough to be tested), **observability** (results are visible), **controllability** (inputs and states can be set), **decomposability** (it can be tested in pieces), **simplicity**, **stability** (changes are infrequent and controlled) and **understandability**.

The overall strategy is a spiral read from the inside out: **unit testing → integration testing → validation testing → system testing**. The scope widens at each turn and so does who runs it — the developer runs unit and most integration tests; an independent test group (ITG) runs validation and system tests; the customer runs acceptance tests.

### Unit testing

The unit is the smallest testable component: a function, a procedure, a class method. What is tested: the **module interface** (parameters in and out), **local data structures**, **boundary conditions**, **independent paths** through the control structure, and all **error-handling paths**.

Because a unit is not a program, it needs scaffolding:

- A **driver** is a "main program" that accepts test data, passes it to the unit under test and prints the results. It **replaces the caller**.
- A **stub** is a dummy that replaces a module the unit under test **calls**. It may do nothing, print a trace, or return a canned value.

**Driver = above, stub = below.** That one line answers most questions on this topic.

### Integration testing

Assembling units reveals interface faults: data lost across an interface, one module adversely affecting another, imprecision accumulated across combined sub-functions, global data structures causing problems.

| Strategy | Order | Scaffolding needed | Character |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Big bang** (non-incremental) | combine everything at once | both, minimal | chaos: faults hard to isolate, correction hard, endless loop of fix-and-retest |
| **Top-down** | main control module first, then downwards **depth-first** or **breadth-first** | **stubs** (the lower modules do not exist yet) | major control and decision points tested early; lower-level processing tested last; stubs may have to do real work |
| **Bottom-up** | lowest-level modules first, combined into **clusters** or **builds** | **drivers** (no caller exists yet) | no stubs needed; the program as an entity does not exist until the last module is added |
| **Sandwich / hybrid** | top-down on the upper layers, bottom-up on the lower layers, meeting at a **target layer** | both | combines the advantages; the usual choice in practice |
| **Regression** | re-run a subset after every change | existing suite | guards against side effects of the fix |
| **Smoke** | build daily and run a rapid "does it catch fire" test | build harness | keeps integration risk visible |

A **critical module** — one that addresses several requirements, has a high level of control, is complex or error-prone, or has definite performance requirements — should be integrated and tested as early as possible, which is an argument for a top-down bias.

**Regression testing** re-runs three kinds of test after a change: a representative sample of all tests, tests that focus on the software functions likely to be affected, and tests on the components that were actually changed. Its purpose is to catch the side effects of a correction, not to re-find the original fault.

## White-box (glass-box, structural) testing

White-box testing derives test cases from the internal structure of the code. Its guarantees are precise: exercise every independent path at least once, exercise all logical decisions on their true and false sides, execute all loops at their boundaries and within their operational bounds, and exercise internal data structures to assure their validity.

### The flow graph

Translate the code into a **flow graph**: each node is one or more sequential statements collapsed together, each edge (link) is a transfer of control. A node containing a condition is a **predicate node** and has two or more edges leaving it. An area bounded by edges and nodes, plus the unbounded area outside the graph, is a **region**.

Compound conditions must be split: `if (a && b)` becomes two predicate nodes, not one, because each simple condition contributes an independent decision.

### Cyclomatic complexity, three ways

McCabe's metric $V(G)$ gives the number of **independent paths** in the basis set and therefore an **upper bound on the number of tests** needed to guarantee that every statement is executed at least once and every condition is exercised both ways.

$$\textbf{(1)} \quad V(G) = E - N + 2P$$

where $E$ is edges, $N$ is nodes and $P$ is connected components — for a single program $P = 1$, so $V(G) = E - N + 2$.

$$\textbf{(2)} \quad V(G) = \text{number of predicate nodes} + 1$$

$$\textbf{(3)} \quad V(G) = \text{number of regions in the planar flow graph}$$

All three must agree; computing two of them is the cheapest possible check on your own arithmetic. Guideline: keep $V(G) \le 10$ per module; above that, the module is a maintenance and testing risk.

An **independent path** is any path through the program that introduces at least one new set of processing statements or a new condition — in flow-graph terms, at least one edge not traversed by any previously defined path. The set of $V(G)$ such paths is a **basis set**.

blocks.title: Worked example — cyclomatic complexity and basis path derivation
blocks.text:
Consider this procedure.

```
 1   read n
 2   i = 1
 3   sum = 0
 4   while (i <= n) {
 5       if (a[i] > 0)
 6           sum = sum + a[i]
 7       else
 8           sum = sum - a[i]
 9       i = i + 1
10   }
11   if (sum > 100)
12       print "high"
13   print sum
```

### Step 1 — build the flow graph

Sequential statements collapse into one node.

| Node | Statements |
|---|---|
| **1** | lines 1–3 (read, initialise) |
| **2** | line 4 — `while` predicate |
| **3** | line 5 — `if` predicate |
| **4** | line 6 — `sum = sum + a[i]` |
| **5** | line 8 — `sum = sum - a[i]` |
| **6** | line 9 — `i = i + 1` (join of 4 and 5) |
| **7** | line 11 — `if` predicate |
| **8** | line 12 — `print "high"` |
| **9** | line 13 — `print sum` (join of 7 and 8) |

Edges:

$$1\!\to\!2,\quad 2\!\to\!3,\quad 2\!\to\!7,\quad 3\!\to\!4,\quad 3\!\to\!5,\quad 4\!\to\!6,\quad 5\!\to\!6,\quad 6\!\to\!2,\quad 7\!\to\!8,\quad 7\!\to\!9,\quad 8\!\to\!9$$

So $E = 11$ and $N = 9$.

### Step 2 — compute $V(G)$ three ways

**(1) Edges and nodes.**
$$V(G) = E - N + 2P = 11 - 9 + 2(1) = \mathbf{4}$$

**(2) Predicate nodes.** The predicate nodes are 2 (`while`), 3 (`if a[i] > 0`) and 7 (`if sum > 100`) — three of them.
$$V(G) = 3 + 1 = \mathbf{4}$$

**(3) Regions.** Draw the graph in the plane. The `while` loop $2 \to 3 \to 4 \to 6 \to 2$ and $2 \to 3 \to 5 \to 6 \to 2$ enclose two bounded areas; the `if` at node 7 with edges $7\to8\to9$ and $7\to9$ encloses a third; plus the unbounded outer region.
$$V(G) = 3 \text{ bounded} + 1 \text{ unbounded} = \mathbf{4}$$

All three agree: $V(G) = 4$.

### Step 3 — derive the basis set

Four independent paths, each adding at least one previously untraversed edge.

| Path | Route | New edges introduced |
|---|---|---|
| **P1** | 1–2–7–9 | $1\!\to\!2$, $2\!\to\!7$, $7\!\to\!9$ |
| **P2** | 1–2–7–8–9 | $7\!\to\!8$, $8\!\to\!9$ |
| **P3** | 1–2–3–4–6–2–7–9 | $2\!\to\!3$, $3\!\to\!4$, $4\!\to\!6$, $6\!\to\!2$ |
| **P4** | 1–2–3–5–6–2–7–9 | $3\!\to\!5$, $5\!\to\!6$ |

Coverage check: the four paths together use $1\!\to\!2$, $2\!\to\!3$, $2\!\to\!7$, $3\!\to\!4$, $3\!\to\!5$, $4\!\to\!6$, $5\!\to\!6$, $6\!\to\!2$, $7\!\to\!8$, $7\!\to\!9$, $8\!\to\!9$ — all 11 edges. ✓

### Step 4 — turn paths into test cases

| Path | Input | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | `n = 0` | prints `0`, no "high" |
| P2 | not realisable by itself — with `n = 0`, `sum = 0`, so `sum > 100` is false | see note |
| P3 | `n = 1, a = [200]` | prints `high`, then `200` (covers P3's loop body plus the P2 edges) |
| P4 | `n = 1, a = [-5]` | prints `-5` |

**Important note.** P2 as written is *not executable* — the loop must run at least once for `sum` to exceed 100. A basis path need not be individually realisable; the basis set is a mathematical construct over the graph. In practice the tester replaces an unrealisable basis path with a realisable path that covers the same new edges, which is what the `n = 1, a = [200]` case does above. Recognising this is what separates a mechanical answer from an understood one.

## Control structure testing

Basis path testing alone is not enough, so three further white-box families refine it.

**Condition testing** exercises the logical conditions in a module. A *simple condition* is $E_1 \langle \text{relational operator} \rangle E_2$ or a boolean variable, possibly negated; a *compound condition* joins simple conditions with `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`. Strategies: **branch testing** (each condition's true and false outcomes, and every simple condition inside a compound one, taken at least once); **domain testing** (for a relational expression $E_1 \langle \text{rel} \rangle E_2$, three tests — $E_1 > E_2$, $E_1 = E_2$, $E_1 < E_2$ — catch relational-operator and expression faults); and **BRO (branch and relational operator) testing**, which uses a condition constraint set to detect branch and relational operator errors.

**Data flow testing** selects paths according to the locations of **definitions** and **uses** of variables. For a statement $S$, $\text{DEF}(S)$ is the set of variables defined there and $\text{USE}(S)$ the set used. A **definition-use (DU) chain** $[X, S, S']$ means $X$ is defined at $S$, used at $S'$, and no intervening statement redefines $X$. The **DU testing strategy** requires every DU chain to be covered at least once.

**Loop testing** focuses on the constructs where the most faults hide.

- **Simple loop** with maximum $n$ passes: skip the loop entirely; **one** pass; **two** passes; $m$ passes where $m < n$; $n-1$, $n$ and $n+1$ passes.
- **Nested loops**: start at the innermost loop, set all outer loops to their minimum values, test the inner one as a simple loop; then work outward, holding the loops already tested at typical values and the outer ones at minimum; continue until all loops are done.
- **Concatenated loops**: if the loops are independent, test each as a simple loop; if the second loop's counter depends on the first, treat them as nested.
- **Unstructured loops**: do not test them — redesign the code to use structured constructs.

Coverage criteria form a hierarchy, each implying the ones above it: **statement coverage** ⊂ **branch (decision) coverage** ⊂ **condition coverage** — with the caution that condition coverage does not always imply branch coverage, which is why **condition/decision coverage** and **MC/DC (modified condition/decision coverage)** are defined; path coverage is the strongest and is usually infeasible.

## Black-box (behavioural, functional) testing

Black-box testing derives test cases from the specification, ignoring internal structure. It attacks categories of error that white-box testing tends to miss: incorrect or missing functions, interface errors, errors in data structures or external database access, behaviour and performance errors, and initialisation and termination errors.

### Equivalence partitioning

Divide the input domain into classes such that any member of a class should be handled identically, then test one value from each class. Guidelines for forming classes: for a **range** $a..b$, one valid class ($a \le x \le b$) and two invalid ones ($x < a$, $x > b$); for a **specific value**, one valid and two invalid classes; for a **set of values**, one valid class per member and one invalid class; for a **boolean**, one valid and one invalid class. The pay-off is a huge reduction in test count for a small loss in fault-finding power.

### Boundary value analysis

Faults cluster at the edges, not in the middle, so test the edges. For a variable with range $a..b$, test $a-1$, $a$, $a+1$, $b-1$, $b$, $b+1$ — and also a nominal value in the middle. The standard test-count formulas for $n$ input variables, with the rule that all variables but one are held at their nominal value:

| Variant | Values tested per variable | Test cases |
|---|---|---|
| **Boundary value analysis (normal)** | $\text{min}, \text{min}^+, \text{max}^-, \text{max}$ | $4n + 1$ |
| **Robust BVA** | adds $\text{min}-1$ and $\text{max}+1$ | $6n + 1$ |
| **Worst-case BVA** | all combinations of 5 values | $5^n$ |
| **Robust worst-case BVA** | all combinations of 7 values | $7^n$ |

The $+1$ in the first two is the single all-nominal test case. These four formulas are asked directly, so memorise the pattern: normal $4n+1$, robust $6n+1$, worst-case $5^n$, robust worst-case $7^n$.

### Cause-effect graphing

Equivalence partitioning and BVA look at inputs one at a time and miss faults that arise from **combinations**. Cause-effect graphing fixes that. The procedure: list the **causes** (input conditions) and **effects** (actions or output conditions) for a module and give each an identifier; build a **cause-effect graph** linking them with the boolean operators identity, NOT, OR and AND, and annotate it with **constraints** (E exclusive, I inclusive/at-least-one, O one-and-only-one, R requires, M masks); convert the graph into a **limited-entry decision table**, each column of which becomes a test case.

### Decision tables

A decision table has four quadrants: **condition stub** and **condition entries** above, **action stub** and **action entries** below. Each column (rule) is a combination of condition outcomes with the actions it triggers. For $n$ binary conditions there are $2^n$ rules before simplification, and each surviving rule becomes one test case. Decision tables are also a component-level *design* notation, which is why they appear in both topics.

### Other black-box techniques

- **Comparison testing (back-to-back)** — run redundant independently developed versions on the same input and compare, used for safety-critical systems.
- **Orthogonal array testing** — for a small input domain with many parameters, select a statistically balanced subset of combinations giving pairwise coverage with far fewer tests than exhaustive testing.
- **State transition testing** — derive tests from a finite state model: valid transitions, invalid transitions, and unreachable states.
- **Error guessing** — experience-driven; not systematic but empirically productive.
- **Graph-based testing** — model objects and their relationships, then cover nodes and links.

## Validation, system and acceptance testing

**Validation testing** begins where integration ends: the software is assembled, interface errors have been removed, and it is tested as a package against the **validation criteria** in the SRS. The outcome of each test is either that the function or performance conforms, or a **deficiency list** entry, negotiated with the customer.

**Alpha and beta testing**, the pair most often confused:

| | Alpha | Beta |
|---|---|---|
| Where | **developer's site** | **customer's / end user's site** |
| Who runs it | the customer or a representative user | end users |
| Developer present? | **yes**, recording errors and usage problems | **no** |
| Environment | controlled | live, uncontrolled |
| Order | first | after alpha |

**Acceptance testing** is the customer's formal validation against the contract; for a product with many customers, alpha and beta testing take its place.

**System testing** exercises the software as part of the whole computer-based system, and has named varieties:

- **Recovery testing** — force failures and verify that recovery is correct: for automated recovery, check reinitialisation, checkpointing, data recovery and restart; for manual recovery, measure MTTR against its specified bound.
- **Security testing** — attempt to penetrate; the tester plays the attacker. The guiding principle is that given enough time and resource, good security testing will *always* break in, so the goal is to make penetration cost more than the information is worth.
- **Stress testing** — demand abnormal quantity, frequency or volume of resource: ten interrupts per second where one or two is normal, input data rates increased by an order of magnitude, maximum memory, thrashing the disk. **Sensitivity testing** is the variant that hunts for the small band of input data inside a valid class that causes instability.
- **Performance testing** — measure run-time performance in an integrated system; it is coupled with stress testing and usually needs instrumentation.
- **Deployment / configuration testing** — exercise the software across each environment it must run in.

**Debugging** is not testing; it follows testing. Its three strategies are **brute force** (memory dumps, run-time traces, print statements — the least efficient and most common), **backtracking** (from the symptom, walk the source backwards until the cause is found; works only for small programs), and **cause elimination** (binary partitioning: form a hypothesis from the data, prove or disprove it, halving the suspect region each time). Debugging outcomes: the cause is found and corrected, or it is not found, and in the latter case the fix that "makes the symptom go away" is the one that later produces two new faults — always ask what other defect the same fix might introduce and what regression tests must be re-run.

blocks.title: Worked example — black-box test design for a date validator
blocks.text:
A function accepts a day $d$, month $m$ and year $y$ and reports whether the date is valid. Constraints: $1 \le d \le 31$, $1 \le m \le 12$, $1900 \le y \le 2100$.

**Equivalence classes for $m$:** valid $\{1..12\}$; invalid $\{m \le 0\}$; invalid $\{m \ge 13\}$. That is 1 valid and 2 invalid classes, matching the range rule. Same shape for $d$ and $y$.

**Normal BVA.** With $n = 3$ variables, the count is $4n + 1 = 4(3) + 1 = \mathbf{13}$ test cases. Taking nominal values $d = 15$, $m = 6$, $y = 2000$:

| # | $d$ | $m$ | $y$ | Which boundary |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 6 | 2000 | $d$ min |
| 2 | 2 | 6 | 2000 | $d$ min$^+$ |
| 3 | 30 | 6 | 2000 | $d$ max$^-$ |
| 4 | 31 | 6 | 2000 | $d$ max |
| 5–8 | 15 | 1, 2, 11, 12 | 2000 | $m$ boundaries |
| 9–12 | 15 | 6 | 1900, 1901, 2099, 2100 | $y$ boundaries |
| 13 | 15 | 6 | 2000 | all nominal |

**Robust BVA** adds $\text{min}-1$ and $\text{max}+1$ for each variable: $6n + 1 = 6(3) + 1 = \mathbf{19}$ test cases, adding $d = 0, 32$; $m = 0, 13$; $y = 1899, 2101$.

**Worst-case BVA** takes all combinations of the five values $\{\text{min}, \text{min}^+, \text{nom}, \text{max}^-, \text{max}\}$ for every variable: $5^n = 5^3 = \mathbf{125}$ test cases. **Robust worst case** gives $7^3 = \mathbf{343}$.

**What all of these miss.** None of them tests 29 February. The rule "29 February is valid iff the year is a leap year" is a *combination* of month, day and year, so it needs **cause-effect graphing** or a **decision table**:

| Condition | R1 | R2 | R3 | R4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $m = 2$ | T | T | T | F |
| $d = 29$ | T | T | F | – |
| $y$ divisible by 4 and (not by 100 or by 400) | T | F | – | – |
| **Action: valid** | ✓ | ✗ | ✓ | (other rules) |

That is the lesson of the technique: partitioning and BVA test each variable's edges, but only a combinational technique catches a rule that spans several variables. It also shows why the day range should really be equivalence-partitioned per month (28/29, 30, 31) rather than treated as a flat 1..31.

blocks.title: Stubs, drivers and which integration needs which
blocks.text:
A **stub** stands in for a module that is **called** by the module under test — it is *below* it in the call hierarchy.
A **driver** stands in for the module that **calls** the module under test — it is *above* it.

Therefore:

| Strategy | Needs |
|---|---|
| **Top-down integration** | **stubs** (the lower levels are not built yet) |
| **Bottom-up integration** | **drivers** (there is no caller yet) |
| **Sandwich** | both |
| **Unit testing a single module** | both, if it calls others and is called |

The question is usually phrased as "top-down integration requires ___", and the wrong answer is always "drivers". Remember: **top-down needs stubs**.

blocks.q: A program's flow graph has 14 edges and 11 nodes and is a single connected component. Its cyclomatic complexity is
blocks.exp: $V(G) = E - N + 2P = 14 - 11 + 2(1) = 5$. Cross-check with the other formulas: the graph must contain 4 predicate nodes ($4 + 1 = 5$) and, drawn in the plane, 5 regions including the unbounded one. Any two of the three formulas agreeing confirms the answer.

blocks.q: A module accepts four independent input variables. The number of test cases required by robust boundary value analysis is
blocks.exp: Robust BVA tests six values per variable (min−1, min, min⁺, max⁻, max, max+1) while holding the other variables at nominal, plus one all-nominal case: $6n + 1 = 6(4) + 1 = 25$. The distractor 17 is normal BVA ($4n+1$), 625 is worst-case BVA ($5^4$) and 2401 is robust worst-case ($7^4$).

blocks.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes alpha and beta testing?
opts: Alpha is at the customer site with the developer absent; beta is at the developer site
Alpha is at the developer site with the developer present; beta is at the customer site with the developer absent
Both are conducted by the development team at the developer site
blocks.exp: Alpha testing is conducted at the developer's site by a customer representative, in a controlled environment, with the developer looking over the shoulder and recording problems. Beta testing happens later at one or more end-user sites, in a live environment, with the developer absent; users report problems back at intervals. The order is alpha then beta.

tricks.title: Compute V(G) two ways, always
tricks.body: Count predicate nodes and add one, then check with $E - N + 2$. They must agree. If they do not, you have either missed an edge or forgotten that a compound condition `if (a && b)` splits into two predicate nodes.

tricks.title: The four BVA counts
tricks.body: Normal $4n+1$, robust $6n+1$, worst case $5^n$, robust worst case $7^n$. The linear forms hold all but one variable at nominal and add one all-nominal case; the exponential forms take all combinations. Spot 'robust' (adds the two out-of-range values) and 'worst case' (combinations) independently.

tricks.title: V(G) is an upper bound on tests, a lower bound on paths
tricks.body: It bounds the number of tests needed for branch coverage from above and the number of paths needed for full path coverage from below. If a question asks 'minimum tests to cover every statement', the answer is usually smaller than $V(G)$ — $V(G)$ answers 'independent paths in the basis set'.

tricks.title: Read the scaffolding question backwards
tricks.body: Ask which end of the hierarchy is missing. Missing children → stubs → top-down. Missing parent → driver → bottom-up. This also settles unit-test questions: a leaf function needs only a driver, an intermediate function needs both.

tricks.title: Verification is static, validation is dynamic
tricks.body: If the activity is a review, inspection, walkthrough or static analysis, it is verification. If it runs the program against user expectations — acceptance, alpha, beta — it is validation. That heuristic handles nearly every V&V option list.

traps.title: Error, fault and failure are three different things
traps.body: A human makes an **error**, which puts a **fault** in the artefact, which on execution may cause a **failure**. A fault that is never executed causes no failure, and a failure can be caused by more than one fault. Options that use the three words interchangeably are wrong by construction.

traps.title: Basis paths need not all be executable
traps.body: The basis set is derived from the graph, not from the semantics, so some paths may be infeasible (a loop guard that cannot be false on the first pass, mutually exclusive conditions). The tester substitutes realisable paths that cover the same edges; the count $V(G)$ does not change.

traps.title: Top-down integration uses stubs, not drivers
traps.body: The mnemonic reads 'top-down, stubs down'. Bottom-up needs drivers because there is nothing above the module to call it. Half the marks on integration questions turn on this one pairing.

traps.title: Condition coverage does not guarantee branch coverage
traps.body: For `if (a || b)`, the two tests (a=T, b=F) and (a=F, b=T) give full condition coverage but take the same branch both times, leaving the false branch untested. That is why condition/decision coverage and MC/DC exist, and why 'condition coverage subsumes decision coverage' is false.

traps.title: Regression testing is not re-running everything
traps.body: Re-running the full suite after every change is usually infeasible. Regression testing selects a representative sample plus tests focused on the changed function and the changed components. An option describing it as 'complete retesting of the entire system' misses the point of selection.

topics.title: Configuration Management, Reuse and Re-engineering
topics.summary: Baselines and SCIs, the five SCM tasks and the change control process, versions versus revisions and variants, maintenance categories, software reuse economics, and re-engineering with reverse engineering and restructuring.

blocks.text:
## Why configuration management exists

The **first law of system engineering**, as Bersoff puts it, is that no matter where you are in the system life cycle, the system will change, and the desire to change it will persist throughout the life cycle. Change is not a failure of planning; it is the permanent condition. Software configuration management (SCM) is the umbrella activity that makes change *controlled* rather than chaotic: it identifies what can change, controls how it changes, ensures the change is properly implemented, and reports the change to everyone who needs to know.

Note the scope boundary that examiners test: **SCM is applied throughout the life cycle** as an umbrella activity, whereas **software maintenance** is a set of engineering activities that occur after the software has been delivered. SCM is not a phase.

### Configuration items and baselines

A **software configuration item (SCI)** is any information item created as part of the software engineering process that is placed under configuration control. The set of SCIs is the **software configuration**, and it is much wider than source code: the system specification, the software project plan, the SRS with prototypes, the design specification with data design and architectural design, source code listings, test plans and procedures and test cases, operation and installation manuals, executable programs, database descriptions, user manuals, maintenance documents (change requests, change reports, engineering change orders), and the standards and procedures for software engineering. Tools used to build the system are increasingly placed under control too, so that a five-year-old release can still be rebuilt.

A **baseline**, in IEEE's words, is a specification or product that has been **formally reviewed and agreed upon**, that thereafter serves as the **basis for further development**, and that can be **changed only through formal change control procedures**. The three-part definition is quoted in questions almost verbatim.

The mechanism is simple and worth picturing. An SCI under development sits in a private workspace where the engineer may change it freely. When it passes a formal technical review it is **approved** and moves into the **project database**, becoming a baseline. From that moment nobody edits it in place: to change it you **check out** a copy (which may lock the master), make the change, have it reviewed, and **check in**, creating a new version. The typical baselines are the System Specification, the Software Requirements Specification, the Design Specification, the Source Code, the Test Plans/Procedures/Data, and the Operational System.

## The five SCM tasks

| Task | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Identification** | name and structure the SCIs, define their relationships, establish an object-oriented naming and evolution scheme |
| **Version control** | combine procedures and tools to manage the versions of configuration objects that are created during the process |
| **Change control** | authorise, evaluate, implement and verify changes to baselined items |
| **Configuration auditing** | confirm that a change has been properly implemented — a formal technical review plus a configuration audit |
| **Status reporting (status accounting)** | tell everyone what changed, who did it, when it happened and what else it affects |

Identification distinguishes **basic objects** (a unit of text created by an engineer — a section of a specification, a source listing, a test case) from **aggregate objects** (a collection of basic objects and other aggregate objects — the *Design Specification* is an aggregate of the data model, component model and interface model). Relationships between objects are recorded as `<part-of>` links and `<interrelated>` links, so that an impact analysis can traverse them.

### Version control, revisions and variants

Three words that are routinely swapped in options:

- A **version** is an instance of a configuration item that differs in some way from other instances. Versions are what version control stores.
- A **revision** is a version created to **correct faults in or improve on** a previous version; it is intended to **replace** its predecessor. Revisions form a sequence — 1.0, 1.1, 1.2 — along an evolution path.
- A **variant** is a version that is **functionally equivalent** but built for a different environment or configuration, and it **co-exists** with its siblings rather than superseding them: the same release compiled for Windows and for Linux, or with and without a particular feature.
- A **release** is a version distributed to customers, as opposed to an internal build.

The picture is an **evolution graph**: a trunk of successive revisions with branches for variants, each node labelled with its version number and attributes. Version control systems use **check-in/check-out** with either **pessimistic locking** (only one writer at a time) or **optimistic concurrency** (parallel edits, merge on check-in).

A **configuration** is a named set of specific versions of SCIs that together make a consistent whole; a **build** produces an executable from a configuration. Conventional numbering `major.minor.patch` maps onto this: a major number change signals incompatible functional change, a minor number signals added functionality, a patch number signals a corrective revision.

## The change control process

Change control balances two opposing needs: uncontrolled change produces chaos, and excessive control produces bureaucracy that engineers route around. The formal sequence for a change to a **baselined** item is:

1. A **change request** is submitted and evaluated for technical merit, potential side effects, overall impact on other configuration objects and system functions, and projected cost.
2. A **change report** records the results of that evaluation.
3. The **change control authority (CCA)** — often a **change control board (CCB)** — makes the final decision on status and priority, weighing the technical and business impact.
4. If approved, an **engineering change order (ECO)** is generated, describing the change to be made, the constraints, and the criteria for review and audit.
5. The object to be changed is **checked out** of the project database; access control and synchronisation control govern who may do so and prevent two engineers from overwriting each other.
6. The change is made, and the modified object is **reviewed** (a formal technical review) and **audited** (a configuration audit).
7. The object is **checked in**, the new version is **baselined** for testing, and after testing the appropriate version is **promoted** and eventually **released**.

Before an item is baselined, only **informal change control** applies — the developer simply makes the change. Between baselining and release, **project-level change control** applies. After release, **formal change control** with a CCB applies. A question asking "what level of change control applies to an object that has not yet been baselined?" wants *informal*.

**Configuration auditing** complements the formal technical review by asking the procedural questions the review does not: was the change specified in the ECO actually made, and were any additional modifications incorporated? Was a formal technical review conducted? Were SCM procedures for noting, recording and reporting the change followed? Have all related SCIs been properly updated?

**Status reporting (CSR)** answers: what happened, who did it, when did it happen, and what else will be affected. Its purpose is to prevent the classic failure in which two people solve the same problem in incompatible ways because neither knew the other was working on it.

The governing standard is **IEEE 828** (Software Configuration Management Plans); IEEE 1042 is its guide.

## Software maintenance

Maintenance consumes between 60% and 70% of the total life-cycle cost of a software product, which is why it, not construction, dominates the economics. Four categories, with their approximate shares from the Lientz and Swanson survey:

| Category | What it is | Share |
|---|---|---|
| **Corrective** | fix defects found after delivery | ~21% |
| **Adaptive** | adjust to a changed environment — new OS, new hardware, new regulation | ~25% |
| **Perfective** (enhancement) | add or improve function at user request | ~50% |
| **Preventive** (re-engineering) | change to improve future maintainability, before a problem occurs | ~4% |

The key reading is that **perfective maintenance is the largest category**, not corrective — maintenance is mostly enhancement, not bug-fixing. Options claiming corrective is the biggest are the standard distractor.

**Lehman's laws of software evolution** describe what happens to a program that is used in a real environment (an *E-type* system):

1. **Continuing change** — it must be continually adapted or it becomes progressively less satisfactory.
2. **Increasing complexity** — as it evolves its complexity increases unless work is done to reduce it.
3. **Self-regulation** — the evolution process is self-regulating, with measures of product and process attributes near normal distributions.
4. **Conservation of organisational stability** — the average effective global activity rate is invariant over the product's lifetime.
5. **Conservation of familiarity** — the incremental growth in each release tends to remain constant.
6. **Continuing growth** — functional content must be continually increased to maintain user satisfaction.
7. **Declining quality** — quality appears to decline unless the system is rigorously maintained and adapted.
8. **Feedback system** — evolution processes are multi-level, multi-loop, multi-agent feedback systems.

Maintainability is measured by **MTTC (mean time to change)**: the average time to analyse a change request, design a modification, implement it, test it and distribute it. Boehm's maintenance effort model uses the **annual change traffic (ACT)** — the fraction of source instructions that undergo change in a year — with $\text{AME} = \text{ACT} \times \text{development effort} \times \text{EAF}$.

## Software reuse

Reuse is the deliberate use of existing assets to build new systems. It pays off in reduced cost and schedule, improved reliability (a component used many times has been tested many times), and reduced process risk — but it imposes its own costs and must be justified numerically.

**Levels of reuse**, from largest unit to smallest:

- **Application system reuse** — reuse the whole application, either unchanged (a COTS product) or as a **product line** with configurable variants.
- **Component reuse** — reuse subsystems or single components.
- **Object and function reuse** — reuse individual classes or library functions.

**The reuse process.** Component-based development qualifies, adapts and composes:

1. **Qualification** — establish that a candidate component really does what is needed, including its interface, performance, reliability and any hidden assumptions.
2. **Adaptation** — wrap or modify the component so that conflicts with its new context are removed. White-box wrapping modifies the internals; grey-box uses an extension language or API; **black-box wrapping** changes only the interface and is the preferred technique.
3. **Composition** — bind components into a working architecture using an infrastructure (a broker, a bus, a framework).
4. **Update** — maintain a component that a third party supplied, usually by requesting a new release rather than editing it.

The counterpart process is **domain engineering** — analysing an application domain, identifying the reusable elements common to its members, and building a reusable library — which runs in parallel with software (application) engineering. Its outputs are a domain analysis model, a structural model and structure points, and the reuse library itself.

**Barriers to reuse**: increased maintenance costs when the source is unavailable; lack of tool support; the *not-invented-here* syndrome; the cost of creating, maintaining and searching a component library; and the difficulty of finding, understanding and adapting a component. A component must be **generic enough to be reusable and specific enough to be useful** — the central tension.

**Reuse metrics** include the percentage of reused LOC or function points, the number of reuses per component, and the **cost of reuse** relative to the cost of building new.

blocks.title: Worked example — is building for reuse worth it?
blocks.text:
Let $C$ be the cost of building a component for a single use. Building the same component to a reusable standard — generalised interface, full documentation, extra testing, no hidden assumptions about its context — typically costs more. Take the common planning figure of a **50% premium**, so the reusable version costs $1.5C$. Each time it is reused, qualification, adaptation and integration cost **20%** of $C$.

**Cost of $n$ applications building it from scratch each time:**
$$\text{Cost}_{\text{new}} = nC$$

**Cost of building it once for reuse and using it $n$ times:**
$$\text{Cost}_{\text{reuse}} = 1.5C + 0.2Cn$$

**Break-even.** Set them equal:
$$1.5C + 0.2Cn = nC \;\Longrightarrow\; 1.5 = 0.8n \;\Longrightarrow\; n = 1.875$$

So reuse pays from the **second** application onwards (since $n$ must be a whole number, $n = 2$ is the first profitable point).

**Check the numbers.**

| $n$ | Build new | Build for reuse | Saving |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $1.0C$ | $1.7C$ | $-0.7C$ (a loss) |
| 2 | $2.0C$ | $1.9C$ | $+0.1C$ |
| 3 | $3.0C$ | $2.1C$ | $+0.9C$ |
| 5 | $5.0C$ | $2.5C$ | $+2.5C$ |
| 10 | $10.0C$ | $3.5C$ | $+6.5C$ |

**Reading the table.** The first user of a reusable component always loses money — which is exactly why reuse programmes fail when the cost is charged to the first project rather than to the organisation. The saving then grows almost linearly, so the decision variable is not whether reuse is cheaper in principle but **how many times you honestly expect the component to be used**.

**A concrete instance.** Suppose $C = \$40{,}000$ and the component is planned for four applications.
$$\text{Cost}_{\text{new}} = 4 \times 40{,}000 = \$160{,}000$$
$$\text{Cost}_{\text{reuse}} = 1.5(40{,}000) + 0.2(40{,}000)(4) = 60{,}000 + 32{,}000 = \$92{,}000$$
$$\text{Saving} = \$68{,}000, \text{ i.e. } 42.5\%$$

**Sensitivity.** If adaptation turns out to cost 50% of $C$ rather than 20% — a badly documented component, or a poor architectural fit — then $\text{Cost}_{\text{reuse}} = 1.5C + 0.5Cn$ and break-even moves to $1.5 = 0.5n$, i.e. $n = 3$. Adaptation cost, not build cost, is what usually destroys the business case.

## Re-engineering

**Business process reengineering (BPR)** sits above software: it redesigns the business processes the software supports, on the principle that automating a bad process only makes it fail faster. Its hierarchy is **business → business system → process → sub-process** and its iterative model is business definition, process identification, process evaluation, process specification and design, prototyping, refinement and instantiation.

**Software re-engineering** is the examination and alteration of a legacy system to reconstitute it in a new form. The **software re-engineering process model** is a cycle of six activities, and the order is examinable:

1. **Inventory analysis** — build a table of every application with its business criticality, current maintainability, longevity, expected change frequency and so on; sort it and pick the candidates. Do not attempt to re-engineer everything.
2. **Document restructuring** — decide how much documentation to recreate; options range from leaving it alone, through documenting only the parts that change, to fully re-documenting a business-critical system.
3. **Reverse engineering** — extract design information from the source code.
4. **Code restructuring** — analyse the source, violations of structured programming are noted and the code is restructured (automatically, in the usual case) while preserving behaviour; then review and test.
5. **Data restructuring** — usually the most far-reaching change, since data architecture drives program architecture: analyse the source code, refine the data model, and migrate the data.
6. **Forward engineering** (also **renovation** or **reclamation**) — recover design information and use it to reconstitute the existing system, improving its quality and adding new capability.

### Reverse engineering

**Reverse engineering** is the process of analysing a program in an effort to create a representation of it at a **higher level of abstraction** than the source code — a design recovery process. Its inputs are the source code (and possibly the executable); its outputs are the design, the data structures and the processing logic. Three dimensions are recovered: **data** (internal data structures and the database), **processing** (from statement-level through component-level to program-level abstraction), and **user interfaces**.

Key properties: reverse engineering **does not change the system**, and it moves from a *lower* level of abstraction to a *higher* one. Its counterpart, forward engineering, moves from a higher level to a lower one. **Restructuring** stays at the *same* level of abstraction — it changes the form of the code or data without changing its behaviour or raising its abstraction. That three-way distinction is the most commonly examined point in this section.

$$\text{reverse engineering: code} \longrightarrow \text{design} \qquad \text{forward engineering: design} \longrightarrow \text{code} \qquad \text{restructuring: code} \longrightarrow \text{better code}$$

Reverse engineering can be **interactive** (a human guides the tool) or automatic; the **directionality** of a tool is one-way (produce information for the maintainer) or two-way (feed the information to a re-engineering tool). Extracting abstractions is easy at the statement level and progressively harder at the component and program levels; the practical limit is that **design intent** — *why* the code is as it is — is generally unrecoverable.

### Economics

Reengineering is justified when the cost of continuing to maintain exceeds the cost of rebuilding. Pressman's cost-benefit form compares the current annual maintenance cost against the re-engineered one over the remaining life, and the standard benefit expression is

$$\text{Cost benefit} = [P_4 - P_3] + [(P_6 - P_7) \times L] - [P_5 \times (P_8/P_9)]$$

where the $P_i$ are the current and re-engineered costs, error rates and lifetimes. In practice the decision rests on four questions: how business-critical is the application, how long will it remain in service, how maintainable is it now, and how much will a rebuild cost?

blocks.title: The abstraction-level test
blocks.text:
One question settles most re-engineering items: **does the abstraction level go up, down or stay the same?**

| Activity | Direction | Does it change the system? |
|---|---|---|
| **Reverse engineering** | up (code → design) | no |
| **Forward engineering** | down (design → code) | yes, produces a new system |
| **Restructuring** | sideways (same level) | yes, form only; behaviour preserved |
| **Re-engineering** | up then down | yes — it is reverse engineering *followed by* forward engineering |

So re-engineering **contains** reverse engineering; they are not synonyms. And restructuring is not reverse engineering, because no higher-level representation is produced.

blocks.q: An SCI that has been formally reviewed and agreed upon, and can subsequently be changed only through formal change control procedures, is called
blocks.exp: That is the IEEE definition of a baseline, in three parts: formally reviewed and agreed, serving as the basis for further development, and changeable only through formal change control. A version is any distinguishable instance of an item, a variant is a functionally equivalent instance for a different environment, and a build is the act of producing an executable from a configuration.

blocks.q: Which sequence correctly orders the change control process for a baselined item?
opts: Change request → ECO → change report → CCA decision → check out
Change request → change report → CCA decision → ECO → check out
ECO → change request → check out → change report → CCA decision
Check out → change request → change report → ECO → CCA decision
blocks.exp: The request is evaluated first, producing a change report that estimates technical merit, side effects, impact and cost. The change control authority then decides, and only if it approves is an engineering change order generated. The object is checked out after the ECO exists, changed, reviewed, audited and checked in.

blocks.q: Re-engineering an existing system differs from reverse engineering in that re-engineering
opts: only recovers design information without altering the system
operates at the same level of abstraction as the source code
recovers design information and then uses it to rebuild the system
is performed before the system is first delivered
blocks.exp: Reverse engineering is a pure analysis activity: it raises the abstraction level from code to design and leaves the system untouched. Re-engineering uses reverse engineering as one of its six activities and then applies forward engineering to reconstitute the system in a better form, so it both recovers and rebuilds. Restructuring, by contrast, is the activity that stays at the same abstraction level.

tricks.title: Revision replaces, variant co-exists
tricks.body: If the new instance is meant to supersede the old one because it fixes or improves it, it is a revision. If both instances remain in service because they serve different environments or configurations, it is a variant. That single test settles every version-control terminology question.

tricks.title: Baseline-before-baseline decides the control level
tricks.body: Not yet baselined → informal change control (the developer just changes it). Baselined but not released → project-level change control. Released → formal change control with a change control board. Read the stem for which side of the baseline the item is on.

tricks.title: Perfective is the biggest maintenance category
tricks.body: The order by share is perfective (~50%) > adaptive (~25%) > corrective (~21%) > preventive (~4%). Candidates guess corrective first; the survey figure says enhancement dominates. Remember the definitions by their triggers: defect → corrective, environment → adaptive, user request → perfective, future maintainability → preventive.

tricks.title: Use the abstraction arrow for re-engineering questions
tricks.body: Up means reverse engineering, down means forward engineering, sideways means restructuring, and up-then-down means re-engineering. Draw the arrow before reading the options.

tricks.title: Reuse break-even is a two-line algebra
tricks.body: With a build premium $p$ (as a multiple of single-use cost) and a per-reuse cost $r$, break-even is $p + rn = n$, i.e. $n = p/(1-r)$. With $p = 1.5$ and $r = 0.2$ that gives $1.5/0.8 = 1.875$, so the second use pays.

traps.title: SCM is not maintenance and not a phase
traps.body: SCM is an umbrella activity applied throughout the life cycle, starting before any code exists; maintenance is a set of activities after delivery. A question asking when SCM begins wants 'at the start of the project', not 'after release'.

traps.title: An SCI is not just source code
traps.body: Specifications, plans, design documents, test cases, manuals, databases, executables and even the tools used to build the system are configuration items. Options restricting the term to programs are wrong.

traps.title: Restructuring is not reverse engineering
traps.body: Restructuring changes the form of code or data while preserving behaviour, at the same abstraction level; it produces no higher-level representation. Reverse engineering produces a design from code and changes nothing. Do not treat the words as synonyms.

traps.title: Configuration audit and technical review answer different questions
traps.body: A formal technical review asks whether the changed SCI is technically correct. A configuration audit asks whether the change specified in the ECO was actually made, whether procedure was followed and whether related SCIs were updated. Both are needed; one does not replace the other.

traps.title: Building for reuse costs more, not less, the first time
traps.body: Generalisation, documentation and extra testing add a premium of roughly 50%, so a single-use project that builds for reuse loses money. Reuse economics only turn positive across several applications, which is why reuse is an organisational investment rather than a project-level optimisation.
